docs.title: Flocon - Debugger for Android, iOS and Flutter
Flocon
docs.text:
Inspect and control your running Android, Kotlin Multiplatform, iOS (Swift) and Flutter apps from a desktop app: network, databases, preferences, files, dashboards, crashes and more. AI agents can drive it too, through MCP.

Get Started Download Desktop App View on GitHub

docs.title: ⚡ Highlights
docs.text:
• Timeline: start here

    Everything your app did, in order, on one screen: network calls, database queries, analytics, logs, crashes. Switch to the graph to see a whole session at a glance.

    Timeline

  • Network

    HTTP (OkHttp, Ktor, URLSession, Dio, http), GraphQL, WebSockets and gRPC, with live mocks, bad network simulation and an image preview.

    HTTP & REST · Mocking · gRPC

  • Storage

    Browse and query your SQLite databases, edit preferences and key-value stores, explore and download the files of your app.

    Databases · Preferences · Files

  • Custom debugging

    Dashboards with buttons and forms, tables, parameterized deeplinks, analytics events and feature flags, all rendered on your desktop.

    Dashboards · Deeplinks · Analytics

  • Observability

    Crash reports with stack traces, accessibility events and WebView traffic.

    Crash reporter · Accessibility · WebView

  • AI agents (MCP)

    Flocon Desktop is an MCP server: let Claude Code, Cursor or Gemini read your network calls, query a database or set a mock.

    MCP overview · Cookbook

  • Four SDKs, one desktop

    Kotlin (Android, KMP), Swift (iOS, macOS) and Flutter SDKs share the same protocol and the same desktop app. Pick yours and connect in minutes.

docs.title: 🏗️ Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Your app, with the Flocon SDK in its debug build, connects to Flocon Desktop over a secure WebSocket (through adb reverse on Android emulators and USB devices, directly on iOS simulators and over Wi-Fi):

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Dev as Developer
    participant App as App + Flocon SDK
    participant Desktop as Flocon Desktop
    participant AI as AI agent (MCP)

    Dev->>App: Uses the app
    App->>Desktop: Network call, DB query, event, crash...
    Desktop-->>Dev: Live view
    Dev->>Desktop: Edits a preference, sets a mock, runs a deeplink
    Desktop->>App: Command
    App-->>Dev: State changed, mocked response
    AI->>Desktop: MCP tool call
    Desktop-->>AI: Data from the app

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text: title: Accessibility Events description: See what TalkBack and VoiceOver get from your app: focus order, content descriptions, announcements.

docs.title: ♿ Accessibility Events
docs.text: Flocon streams the accessibility events of your application to the desktop, so you can check the focus order, the content descriptions, the announcements and the live-region updates without listening to a screen reader.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
The Accessibility plugin is available in the Kotlin / KMP SDK only. The Swift and Flutter SDKs do not have it yet.

Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Automatic capture ✅ ✅ (iOS partial, JVM and Wasm manual only) ❌ ❌ Manual log() / announce() ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌ Move the focus from the desktop ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ Platform Capture How Limits Android Automatic Clicks: a touch observer on the window of each activity, always on. Other events: an accessibility delegate on the decor view, plus the AccessibilityManager state listeners Clicks are captured without any accessibility service. The other events are only emitted when TalkBack or another accessibility service is on. Taps only (no keyboard, long press or drag). Dialogs, popups and toasts (windows without an activity) are not covered iOS (KMP) Partial Notifications for the focused element and the finished announcements, plus the VoiceOver and Switch Control status Needs VoiceOver on. Notifications posted by the app itself (screen or layout changes) cannot be observed: use log() JVM (desktop) Manual only log() / announce() The desktop shows that automatic capture is not supported Wasm (browser) Manual only log() / announce() The desktop shows that automatic capture is not supported

docs.title: Setup
Usage
docs.text:
KotlinSwiftFlutter

On Android, nothing to call: taps appear on the desktop right away. Turn on TalkBack on the device (or an emulator) and move the focus in your app to also get the focus, announcement and window events.

On the other platforms, or for the events the automatic capture cannot see, use the manual API:

Flocon.accessibilityPlugin.log(
    AccessibilityEvent(
        type = "VIEW_FOCUSED",
        text = "Add to cart",
        contentDescription = "Add to cart",
        className = "Button",
        screen = "CartScreen",
        bounds = "[48,1530][1032,1674]",
        extras = mapOf("hint" to "Double tap to add"),
    )
)

// the text your app announces to a screen reader, logged as an ANNOUNCEMENT event
Flocon.accessibilityPlugin.announce("Item added to the cart")

log also accepts a List<AccessibilityEvent>.

Not available in the Swift SDK yet

Not available in the Flutter SDK yet

docs.title: Clicks on Android (CLICK)
docs.text:
Flocon observes the touches of each activity window (it never consumes or alters them). When a tap ends on a clickable View or Compose element, it sends a CLICK event describing what a screen reader would read for that element: text, content description and role. A tap on nothing clickable, a scroll or a long press sends nothing.

Extras of a CLICK event:

Extra Meaning source view or compose viewId Resource entry name of the View (Views only) testTag Test tag of the node (Compose only) stateDescription State description of the node (Compose only) clickLabel Label of the click action (Compose only) enabled true or false missingLabel true when the element is clickable but has no text and no content description: a screen reader cannot name it. The desktop shows a warning on these rows

Compose is detected at runtime, the SDK does not add it to your app. VIEW_CLICKED (sent by the platform) still appears when a service is on, next to CLICK.

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
Each event shows:

  • Type: what happened, e.g. CLICK, VIEW_FOCUSED, VIEW_CLICKED, WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED, ANNOUNCEMENT
  • Text & content description: what the screen reader reads
  • Class & screen: the element class and the activity it belongs to
  • Bounds: the position of the element on screen
  • Extras: platform details (hint, traits, assistive technology...)

Filter the list by type or with a text, and clear the events to isolate the next interaction.

The desktop also shows the state of the device: is an accessibility service on, is touch exploration on, which services. When no screen reader is on, the desktop tells you to turn on TalkBack or VoiceOver.

docs.title: Move the focus from the desktop
docs.text:
The top of the Accessibility panel shows the element the screen reader is on (text or content description, class, bounds, and its position in the focus order of the screen). The previous / next buttons move the accessibility focus on the device, like a swipe left / right with TalkBack, and the refresh button asks where the focus is now.

  • A TalkBack remote (collapsible, draggable) also shows whether TalkBack is on and lets you turn it on or off from the desktop when the permission is granted. Over Wi-Fi, the desktop gives you the adb command to grant it once.
  • Android only, and only while TalkBack (or another accessibility service) is on. The buttons are disabled otherwise.
  • The SDK builds the focus order of the resumed activity itself (Views, and the merged semantics tree of Compose), so it can differ slightly from TalkBack's. It does not wrap around: next on the last element does nothing.
  • Dialogs, popups and other windows without an activity are not covered.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_accessibility_events: the events, newest first, filterable by type and text.
  • get_accessibility_state: whether capture is supported, a screen reader is running, touch exploration and the running services. Use it when the list is empty.
  • get_accessibility_focused_node: the element TalkBack is on, with its position in the focus order (Android, TalkBack on).
  • move_accessibility_focus: moves the focus to the next or previous element and returns where it landed (Android, TalkBack on).
  • clear_accessibility_events: deletes the received events.

"Walk the focus order of the checkout screen and list the elements that have no label."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: 💻 ADB Commander
docs.text:
The ADB Commander is a desktop-only tool to run adb commands on your Android devices without leaving Flocon: no terminal, no -s <serial> to type.

There is nothing to add to your app, and no Kotlin, Swift or Flutter SDK is involved: it works with any Android device visible by adb devices. Commands also appear in the timeline as ADB commands.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In the Timeline

Executed commands also show up in the Timeline.

From the desktop UI, you can:

  • Run any command: type it with or without the adb prefix (shell pm list packages -3), the output is displayed in the console.
  • Quick commands: pick a ready-made command (device info, app management, input events…) and fill its [placeholders].
  • Saved commands: star a command to keep it in your library and run it again in one click.
  • History: re-run any of your recent commands.
  • Automation flows: chain several commands into a named flow, with an optional label and delay for each step, then run it, follow the result of every step, and cancel it while it runs.
  • Copy: copy the command or its output with one click.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The ADB Commander only needs a working adb:

  1. Install the Android SDK Platform Tools.
  2. Open Settings in Flocon Desktop and check the ADB path (Flocon tries to find it automatically).
  3. Connect your device: commands target the device selected in the top bar, or every connected device when none is selected.

Tip

The ADB Commander does not need the Flocon SDK in your app: it works with any Android device visible by adb devices.

See Troubleshooting › ADB Connection Issues if your device is not detected.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Android only: it runs adb, so iOS devices and simulators are not supported.
  • Not available for devices connected over Wi-Fi: the desktop shows "ADB is not available for devices connected over wifi".

docs.title: 📊 Analytics Event Viewer
docs.text:
Flocon streams and displays the analytics events emitted by your app in real time, so developers, QA engineers and product teams can verify tracking payloads without opening a dashboard on the analytics provider's side. Each provider (Firebase, Segment, a custom tracker...) is its own table.

Every recorded event shows:

  • Event Name: the tracking identifier.
  • Parameters & Properties: the full key-value dictionary.
  • Timestamp & Source: when it was logged and the stream (table) it belongs to, for example firebase, segment or a custom one.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Log events (one table per stream) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

Property values are always strings.

docs.title: Setup
Usage
docs.text: The stream is the table the events appear in on the desktop. Use one stream per analytics provider to check what each of them receives (firebase, segment, app_telemetry...).

docs.title: Log events
docs.text:
KotlinSwiftFlutter

Log individual or batched events; analyticsTableId is the stream:

import io.github.openflocon.flocon.Flocon
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.analytics.analyticsPlugin
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.analytics.model.AnalyticsEvent
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.analytics.model.analyticsProperty

Flocon.analyticsPlugin.log(
    AnalyticsEvent(
        eventName = "button_clicked",
        analyticsTableId = "firebase",
        "button_id" analyticsProperty "checkout_pay",
        "cart_total" analyticsProperty "49.99",
        "currency" analyticsProperty "EUR"
    )
)

To log several events to the same stream, create a sender once and reuse it:

val firebase = Flocon.analyticsPlugin.sender("firebase")

firebase.log("button_clicked", "button_id" analyticsProperty "checkout_pay")

Flocon.analyticsPlugin.sender("firebase").logEvents(
    AnalyticsEvent(
        eventName: "button_clicked",
        AnalyticsProperty("button_id", "checkout_pay"),
        AnalyticsProperty("cart_total", "49.99"),
        AnalyticsProperty("currency", "EUR")
    )
)

logEvents also takes an array of events. Keep the sender to reuse it:

let firebase = Flocon.analyticsPlugin.sender("firebase")
firebase.logEvents(AnalyticsEvent(eventName: "app_opened"))

Flocon.analytics.sender('firebase').logEvents([
  AnalyticsEvent(
    eventName: 'button_clicked',
    properties: [
      AnalyticsProperty('button_id', 'checkout_pay'),
      AnalyticsProperty('cart_total', '49.99'),
      AnalyticsProperty('currency', 'EUR'),
    ],
  ),
]);

For a single event, the sender also has log:

final firebase = Flocon.analytics.sender('firebase');
firebase.log('app_opened');

docs.title: Generic analytics forwarder
docs.text:
Forward all your app's tracking calls to Flocon alongside your existing provider. The sender is bound to one stream, so you do not repeat it at each call.

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
class AnalyticsTracker(private val firebaseAnalytics: FirebaseAnalytics) {

    // bound to the "app_telemetry" stream: no need to repeat it at each call
    private val flocon = Flocon.analyticsPlugin.sender("app_telemetry")

    fun track(event: String, parameters: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap()) {
        // 1. Forward to Flocon Desktop
        flocon.log(
            eventName = event,
            properties = parameters.map { it.key analyticsProperty it.value.toString() }
        )

        // 2. Forward to Firebase
        val bundle = Bundle().apply {
            parameters.forEach { (k, v) -> putString(k, v.toString()) }
        }
        firebaseAnalytics.logEvent(event, bundle)
    }
}

final class AnalyticsTracker {
    // bound to the "app_telemetry" stream: no need to repeat it at each call
    private let flocon = Flocon.analyticsPlugin.sender("app_telemetry")

    func track(_ event: String, parameters: [String: Any] = [:]) {
        // 1. Forward to Flocon Desktop
        flocon.logEvents(
            AnalyticsEvent(
                eventName: event,
                properties: parameters.map { AnalyticsProperty($0.key, "\($0.value)") }
            )
        )

        // 2. Forward to your analytics provider
        provider.track(event, parameters)
    }
}

class AnalyticsTracker {
  // bound to the "app_telemetry" stream: no need to repeat it at each call
  final _flocon = Flocon.analytics.sender('app_telemetry');

  void track(String event, [Map<String, Object> parameters = const {}]) {
    // 1. Forward to Flocon Desktop
    _flocon.log(event, [
      for (final entry in parameters.entries) AnalyticsProperty(entry.key, '${entry.value}'),
    ]);

    // 2. Forward to your analytics provider
    provider.track(event, parameters);
  }
}

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

Each event also shows up in the Timeline, in the Analytics lane of the graph.

Open Analytics in the sidebar.

  • The table selector switches between streams, the filter field matches event names and properties.
  • Click an event to open its full payload in the detail panel.
  • Right-click an event to Remove it, Remove lines above, Exclude its name, or Clear old sessions (the events of previous app launches).
  • The trash icon clears the events of the selected table. The overflow menu has Export CSV, Auto scroll, Invert list and Clear old sessions.

docs.title: Excluding noisy events
docs.text:
Right-click an event row and choose Exclude (followed by the event name in quotes) to hide every event with that name. An N excluded button then appears next to the filter field: open it to restore one event name, or Restore all.

  • Exclusions are saved per app (package name) and kept when you restart Flocon.
  • Events are only hidden from the list. They are not deleted, and Export CSV still includes them.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_analytics_tables: the streams (tables) of the app.
  • list_analytics_events: the events, newest first, filtered by table, event names, text or time.
  • count_analytics_events: the number of events per event name, most frequent first.

By default only the current app launch is read; pass includeOldSessions to include previous ones.

"Count the analytics events of the last session and tell me which event is sent too often."

"Was checkout_completed sent with a currency property after I paid?"

docs.title: 📉 Bad Network Simulation
docs.text:
Testing on a fast Wi-Fi hides bugs. Flocon can slow down and randomly break the calls of your app from the desktop, without touching the network settings of your device. Use it to check your loaders, timeouts, retries and error screens.

A profile describes how the network misbehaves. Only one profile is active at a time, and it applies to every call the interceptors handle.

docs.title: What a profile contains
docs.text:
• Latency: a trigger probability (the share of calls that get delayed, from 0 to 1) and a min / max latency in milliseconds. The delay of each call is picked in that range.
  • Error probability: the share of calls that fail.
  • Errors: the list of errors a failing call can get. Each one has a weight: the higher it is compared to the others, the more often it is picked. An error is either:
    • an HTTP error: a status code, a body and a content type, returned as the response;
    • an exception: a class to throw, such as java.net.SocketTimeoutException, java.net.UnknownHostException, java.net.ConnectException, javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException or java.io.IOException.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter HTTP calls ✅ OkHttp, Ktor ✅ Ktor (and OkHttp on JVM) ✅ URLSession ✅ Dio, package:http gRPC calls ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌
  • On Android, gRPC calls get the latency and the exception errors. The HTTP errors of a profile are ignored for gRPC. See gRPC.
  • On Swift and Flutter, the exception class of the profile is turned into the closest native error (URLError on Swift, DioException on Dio). A timeout class gives a timeout, a connection class a connection error.
  • The active profile is saved on the device, and applies from the next launch too.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
There is nothing specific to add: the simulation uses the network setup. Any call that goes through the Flocon interceptor is affected.

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
startFlocon(FloconContext(context)) {
    install(FloconNetwork)
}
OkHttpKtorgRPC 
val okHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(FloconOkhttpInterceptor())
    .build()

val httpClient = HttpClient {
    install(FloconKtorPlugin)
}

Android only, with flocon-grpc-interceptor or flocon-grpc-interceptor-lite (see gRPC):

val channel = ManagedChannelBuilder.forAddress(host, port)
    .intercept(FloconGrpcInterceptor())
    .build()

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.network)
}
#endif

let session = URLSession(configuration: .default.withFlocon())

The simulation applies to URLSession.shared and to the sessions created with withFlocon(). A request excluded by shouldLog is not affected.

await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon..install(FloconNetwork()));

final dio = Dio().withFlocon();             // flocon_dio
final client = http.Client().withFlocon();  // flocon_http

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
1. Open the Network tab and click the Bad network button in the toolbar.
  2. Create a profile: set the latency (trigger probability, min and max), the error probability, and add errors (HTTP errors or exceptions, each with a weight).
  3. Turn the profile on with its switch. Turning another one on turns the first one off, and turning the active one off stops the simulation.
  4. Use your app. Calls are delayed or fail according to the profile.

docs.title: Scenarios to try
docs.text:
• Subway (intermittent drops): error probability 0.4, with a java.net.SocketTimeoutException and a java.net.UnknownHostException. Check that the app shows a retry banner instead of crashing.
  • Slow 3G: trigger probability 1, latency between 2000 and 5000 ms. Check loaders, skeletons and cancellation when leaving a screen.
  • Backend outage: error probability 1, with one HTTP error 503. Check the maintenance screen.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_bad_network_configs: lists the profiles and tells which one is active.
  • create_bad_network_config, update_bad_network_config, delete_bad_network_config: manage the profiles.
  • set_active_bad_network_config: activates a profile (the others are turned off), or turns the simulation off when no profile is given.

"Simulate a flaky network with 30% of timeouts, then check that the login screen handles it."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The simulation does not throttle bandwidth: it adds latency and errors to calls.
  • It cannot target a domain or a path. To break one endpoint only, use a mock.
  • WebSocket frames are not affected.

docs.title: Connect with a QR code
docs.text: Instead of typing the address of your computer, scan it. The device and the computer must be on the same network, as for a Wi-Fi connection.

docs.title: 1. Show the QR code on the desktop
docs.text:
Click the Connect button (laptop icon) in the top bar of Flocon Desktop. If your computer has several networks, pick the one your phone is on.

The QR code holds the IP address of your computer, followed by both ports (ip:ws:http) as soon as one of them is not the default.

docs.title: 2. Scan it from the app
docs.text:
Add a scanner to your app (in a debug menu, for example). Once the code is read, the SDK calls Flocon.connect with the address for you.

KotlinSwiftFlutter

Android only. Add flocon-qr-scanner (and its -no-op in release), then call:

import io.github.openflocon.flocon.qrscanner.scanQrCodeAndConnect

val result = Flocon.scanQrCodeAndConnect(context) // suspend, null when the user closes the scanner

It opens the Google code scanner, so it needs no camera permission but requires Google Play Services; without it, the result is FloconConnectResult.Failed and you connect with the address instead.

FloconQRScannerView (AVFoundation, no extra dependency) reads the QR code and calls Flocon.connect(address:) for you. Your app needs NSCameraUsageDescription; the simulator has no camera, use Flocon.connect(address:) there.

.sheet(isPresented: $isScanning) {
    FloconQRScannerView { result in
        if result == .connected { isScanning = false }
    }
}

Add the flocon_qr_scanner package (Android, iOS, macOS):

flutter pub add flocon_qr_scanner

FloconQrScannerView(onResult: (result) {
  if (result is FloconConnectResultConnected) Navigator.pop(context);
})

It needs the camera permission: NSCameraUsageDescription (iOS, macOS), CAMERA (Android) and com.apple.security.device.camera (macOS entitlements). On Android, mobile_scanner needs minSdk 23, compileSdk 36 and the Android Gradle plugin 8.9.1 or higher.

If the app does not connect after the scan, see Connect over Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Connect over Wi-Fi
docs.text:
A physical device on Wi-Fi has no adb reverse: give the SDK the IP address of your computer. The device and the computer must be on the same network.

To find the address, click the Connect button (laptop icon) in the top bar of Flocon Desktop: it lists the local addresses of your computer, with a Copy address button. Or skip typing it and scan the QR code.

docs.title: Give the address to the SDK
docs.text:
Pass it at start, or later (from a debug menu, for example) with Flocon.connect:

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
startFlocon(FloconContext(this)) {
    connect {
        address = "192.168.1.10"  // host, host:ws or host:ws:http
    }
    install(FloconNetwork)
}

// or, once the address is known
val result = Flocon.connect("192.168.1.10")   // suspend, returns a FloconConnectResult
Flocon.disconnect()                            // suspend, forgets the address

connect { } also has bufferCapacity (messages kept while not connected) and rememberLastAddress (the last connected address is tried again at the next launch and wins over address, true by default).

Flocon.initialize(config: FloconConfig(host: "192.168.1.20"))

// or with the builder
#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.config(host: "192.168.1.20")
    flocon.install(.network)
}
#endif

// or later, once the address is known
let result = await Flocon.connect(address: "192.168.1.20") // FloconConnectResult
await Flocon.disconnect()

On iOS, the app needs NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription in Info.plist, and the user must allow the local network prompt shown the first time (see Troubleshooting).

await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon
  ..connect(host: '192.168.1.20')
  ..install(FloconNetwork()));

// or later, once the address is known
final result = await Flocon.connect('192.168.1.20'); // FloconConnectResult
await Flocon.disconnect();

The desktop shows a wifi icon next to a device connected by address.

docs.title: The address format
docs.text: An address is the IP address or host of your computer, with optional ports: host, host:ws or host:ws:http, for example 192.168.1.20:10023:10024. No scheme, no path. Ports go from 1 to 65535; an omitted port is the configured one (9023 / 9024 by default, see Ports), and the ports in the address win for that address. Anything else (a scheme, more than two ports...) is an invalid address: the connect call returns an InvalidAddress result instead of throwing.

docs.title: When it does not connect
docs.text:
• Guest or corporate Wi-Fi often isolates devices from each other ("client isolation"): use a personal hotspot, or USB for Android.
  • A VPN or a firewall on your computer can block the ports 9023 and 9024.
  • Several network interfaces (Ethernet + Wi-Fi, VPN...): pick the address of the network your phone is on in the Connect dialog.

More in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Automatic connection
docs.text: title: Connect your app description: How an app with the Flocon SDK reaches Flocon Desktop: automatically on emulators, simulators and USB devices, by address or QR code over Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Connect your app
docs.text: Start Flocon Desktop, then run your app. The SDK connects in the background and retries every 3 seconds. Until a desktop is reachable, what the app logs is kept in memory (5000 messages by default, the oldest are dropped) and sent in order once connected.

docs.title: Automatic connection
docs.text:
In most setups there is nothing to do:

Where the app runs What to do Android emulator (Kotlin) Nothing. The SDK uses localhost and the desktop runs adb reverse for you. Android device over USB (Kotlin) Nothing (adb reverse too). USB debugging must be on and adb devices must list it. iOS Simulator, macOS app, JVM desktop app Nothing. localhost is the default. Flutter on an Android emulator Use the host 10.0.2.2, see below. Physical device over Wi-Fi (Android or iOS) Give the SDK the address of your computer: over Wi-Fi or by scanning a QR code.

For Android, the desktop needs adb in your PATH (it comes with the Android SDK platform-tools) to reach emulators and USB devices.

Flutter on an Android emulator: the emulator reaches your computer at 10.0.2.2, and the Flutter SDK does not run adb reverse:

await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon
  ..connect(host: Platform.isAndroid ? '10.0.2.2' : 'localhost')
  ..install(FloconNetwork()));

docs.title: Follow the connection
docs.text:
Turn on the SDK logs to see the attempts: FloconLogger.enabled = true (Kotlin), Flocon.isLoggingEnabled = true (Swift, Flutter), set before starting. In your app, the connection state is exposed as:

SDK API States Kotlin Flocon.connectionState, a StateFlow<FloconConnectionState> (import io.github.openflocon.flocon.connectionState) Idle, Buffering, Connecting, Connected, Failed(reason) Swift Flocon.connectionState or the Flocon.connectionStates stream .idle, .buffering, .connecting, .connected, .failed(reason) Flutter Flocon.connectionState or the Flocon.connectionStates stream idle, buffering, connecting, connected, failed

Keep the SDK and the desktop up to date together

The SDK connects with wss:// / https:// and the desktop no longer serves the plain ports, so an old SDK cannot connect to a new desktop, and the other way around. Flocon Desktop shows an SDK update badge in the top bar when the connected app runs an older SDK than the latest release.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Flocon Desktop listens on three ports:

Port Default Used for WebSocket 9023 the SDK connection HTTP 9024 file uploads of the Files feature MCP 9042 the MCP server for AI agents (fixed)

If 9023 or 9024 are taken on your machine, change them in the desktop under Settings > Server ports (between 1024 and 65535, different from each other, and not 9042). The SDK must then use the same ports, except on an Android emulator or USB device with the Kotlin SDK, where the desktop's adb reverse maps the default 9023 / 9024 to the desktop ports:

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
startFlocon(FloconContext()) {
    connect {
        address = "192.168.1.10"
        websocketPort = 3030
        httpPort = 3031
    }
}

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.config(host: "192.168.1.20", webSocketPort: 3030, httpPort: 3031)
    flocon.install(.network)
}
#endif

await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon
  ..connect(host: '192.168.1.20', webSocketPort: 3030, httpPort: 3031));

Silent failure

If the SDK ports differ from the desktop ones where adb reverse is not used (Wi-Fi device, iOS, JVM, Wasm, Flutter), the app simply never connects, with no error. Turn on the SDK logs to see the attempts.

Launch options. The desktop can also override the ports for the current session only (never saved):

Port Argument Environment variable WebSocket --websocket-port=<n> (or --websocket-port <n>) FLOCON_WEBSOCKET_PORT HTTP --http-port=<n> (or --http-port <n>) FLOCON_HTTP_PORT

The priority for each port is: argument, environment variable, port saved in Settings > Server ports, default. If the resulting ports are invalid, or a value is not a number, the desktop prints the reason on stderr and exits with code 1 without opening a window. An overridden port is disabled in Settings > Server ports.

# macOS, installed app
open -a Flocon --args --websocket-port=9100 --http-port=9101

# from the sources
./gradlew :composeApp:run --args="--websocket-port=9100 --http-port=9101"

With open -a, the environment variables of your shell are not forwarded to an already installed app: prefer the arguments.

Something not connecting? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: 💥 Crash Reporter
docs.text: Flocon records the uncaught crashes of your app (type, message, stack trace and time) and displays them in the desktop app, even when the crash happened while the desktop was not connected. On Android and JVM the previous crash handlers keep working, so Crashlytics, Sentry and friends still see the crash.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Uncaught Kotlin / Java exceptions ✅ ✅ (iOS, JVM) ❌ ❌ Uncaught Dart / Flutter errors ❌ ❌ ❌ ✅ NSException and crash signals (Swift runtime errors, SIGSEGV...) ❌ ❌ ✅ ❌
  • Kotlin: Android, iOS and JVM. On Wasm the plugin does nothing (no crash is saved or sent).
  • Swift: Objective-C exceptions (NSException) and the signals SIGTRAP, SIGABRT, SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGILL, SIGFPE. That covers Swift runtime errors (force unwrap of nil, fatalError, index out of range...). The Swift error message is only printed in the console.
  • Flutter: only the errors caught by FlutterError.onError (framework errors: build, layout, gestures...) and PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError (uncaught asynchronous errors). Native crashes are not reported.

docs.title: Setup
Usage
docs.text:
Nothing to call: once installed, crashes are captured automatically.

  1. The plugin registers its handlers. On Android and JVM the previous ones are kept and still called, so the app crashes as usual. On iOS (KMP) it replaces the Kotlin/Native unhandled-exception hook, then terminates the app.
  2. The crash is saved on the device.
  3. On the next connection to Flocon Desktop, the saved crashes are sent and deleted from the device.
KotlinSwiftFlutter

To install the handler yourself, disable the automatic setup and call setupCrashHandler():

startFlocon(FloconContext(context)) {
    install(FloconCrashReporter) {
        catchFatalErrors = false
    }
}

// later
Flocon.crashReporterPlugin.setupCrashHandler()

A crash cannot be sent while the app crashes: it is saved and sent the next time the app connects. Crashes are not caught while the Xcode debugger is attached, because the debugger catches them first: launch the app from the simulator or the device, without the debugger, to try it.

The hooks are installed by install(FloconCrashReporter()). Errors are saved on disk and sent on the next connection, even after a restart.

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

Crashes also show up in the Timeline: open it to see what the app did right before.

  • Crash list of the selected app, newest first, with the exception type, message and time. Use the search field to filter on type, message or frame.
  • Detail: type, date and message, then two tabs: Stack trace (with a Crashed in your code block on top, and a My code / All frames switch that hides the framework frames) and Raw. A Suppressed tab shows the suppressed exceptions when there are some.
  • Actions: copy the stack trace, delete the selected crash, or delete all the crashes of the app.
  • Crashes also appear in the timeline, so you can read what happened right before.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_crash_reports: crashes of the app (type and message), newest first, filterable by text and date.
  • get_crash_report: full details of one crash, with its stack trace.

"Why did the app crash? Read the last crash report and the timeline just before it."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Crashes are sent on the next connection: the app cannot send them while it crashes.
  • Flutter does not report native crashes. Kotlin does not report native (NDK) crashes either.

docs.title: 📈 Reactive Custom Dashboards
docs.text:
Your app declares custom dashboards (sections of texts, buttons, inputs, JSON, Markdown...) and Flocon Desktop renders them as interactive controls. When your data changes the dashboard updates live, and when you click a button or submit a field on the desktop, a callback runs inside your app.

Use cases:

  • Toggle mock environments or debug options.
  • Display live business metrics, session data or tokens.
  • Change a state value on the fly without rebuilding.
  • Trigger in-app test actions (clear a cache, seed test data, fire a notification).

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Dashboards ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

Every SDK supports the same elements:

Element Kotlin Swift Flutter Description Text text FloconText FloconText Read-only label: value, with an optional ARGB color. Label label FloconLabel FloconLabel A heading or a status line, with an optional ARGB color. Button button FloconButton FloconButton Runs a callback in your app when clicked. Text field textField FloconTextField FloconTextField Sends the entered text to your app on submit. Check box checkBox FloconCheckBox FloconCheckBox Sends the new boolean to your app on change. Plain text plainText FloconPlainText FloconPlainText Multi-line selectable text (logs, dumps). JSON json FloconJSON FloconJson A JSON string, formatted. Markdown markdown FloconMarkdown FloconMarkdown Rendered Markdown. HTML html FloconHTML FloconHtml A styled HTML snippet. Form form FloconForm FloconForm A group of inputs with one submit button.

What drives a reactive section differs per platform:

Reactive section Stop updating Kotlin a Flow<T> cancel the returned Job, or the CoroutineScope you passed Swift a Combine Publisher (such as a @Published property) release or cancel() the returned FloconDashboardHandle Flutter a ValueListenable<T> (FloconSection.listen) or a Stream<T> (FloconSection.fromStream) dispose() the returned FloconDashboardHandle

A dashboard is sent once every reactive section has emitted a first value, and sent again each time one emits and on each connection to the desktop.

docs.title: Setup
Reactive dashboard
Static dashboard
Multi-input forms
docs.text:
A form groups inputs under a single submit button. The callback receives the values of all the inputs, keyed by their id, with check boxes as "true" or "false".

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
Flocon.dashboardPlugin.dashboard(id = "settings", scope = scope) {
    form(
        name = "Server Configuration",
        submitText = "Apply Settings",
        onSubmitted = { values ->
            val host = values["host_input"]
            val mockMode = values["mock_mode"] == "true"
            applyNewConfig(host, mockMode)
        },
    ) {
        textField(id = "host_input", label = "API Host", placeHolder = null, value = "https://staging.api.com")
        checkBox(id = "mock_mode", label = "Enable Mock Mode", value = false)
    }
}

Flocon.dashboardPlugin.dashboard(id: "settings") {
    FloconForm("Create user", submitText: "Create", onSubmitted: { values in
        session.createUser(name: values["name"] ?? "", isAdmin: values["admin"] == "true")
    }) {
        FloconTextField(id: "name", label: "Name", value: "")
        FloconCheckBox(id: "admin", label: "Admin", value: false)
    }
}

Flocon.dashboard.dashboard('settings', [
  FloconForm('Create user', [
    FloconTextField(id: 'name', label: 'Name', value: ''),
    FloconCheckBox(id: 'admin', label: 'Admin', value: false),
  ], submitText: 'Create', onSubmitted: (values) => session.createUser(values['name'] ?? '', values['admin'] == 'true')),
]);

Element ids must be unique

The id of a button, text field, check box or form input must be unique inside its dashboard: it is how the desktop tells your app which element was used.

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
Open Dashboards in the sidebar.

  • One tab per dashboard, named after its id. Click a tab to switch, click its x to remove that dashboard, or use the trash icon (Delete Dashboards) to remove the current one.
  • Each section or form is a card. Texts, labels, check boxes and text fields are laid out in the card; interacting with them calls your app back.
  • A plain text or JSON element has an Open in external editor button to read long content comfortably.
  • The Auto / 1 / 2 / 3 switch at the top right sets how many cards are shown per row.

A dashboard stays until you remove it. Sending a dashboard with an existing id replaces it.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_dashboards: the ids of the dashboards sent by the app.
  • get_dashboard: one dashboard with its sections and elements (texts, values, check boxes, fields, buttons).

The MCP tools are read only: an agent can read what a dashboard shows, but it cannot click a button or submit a form.

"What is the value of the Environment text in the main dashboard?"

"List the dashboards of the app and tell me which options are enabled in settings."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: 🧩 Database Explorer & SQL Editor
docs.text: Flocon lists the SQLite databases of your app (Room, SQLDelight, Core Data stores, sqflite, plain SQLite files) and lets you browse their schema, run SQL queries on them from the desktop and see the queries your app runs, in real time. It helps you check what is really stored, test a query before writing it in code, and spot slow or unexpected queries.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Automatic detection of SQLite files ✅ (with room()) ✅ iOS (Documents, Library), JVM with room { path(...) }, ❌ Wasm ✅ (Documents, Application Support) ✅ (databases, documents, support folders) Browse schema and run SQL ✅ ✅ (Wasm: Room 3 only) ✅ ✅ Query logging ✅ (Room, SQLDelight, manual) ✅ (Room 3, SQLDelight, manual) ✅ (manual) ✅ (manual) Transactions grouped in the logs ✅ (Room) ✅ (Room 3) ❌ ❌
  • Wasm has no file system and no SQLite file: only Room 3 with WebWorkerSQLiteDriver can be registered. The SQLDelight web worker driver is not supported yet.
  • Swift and Flutter open the SQLite file itself, whatever library wrote it (Core Data, GRDB, SQLite.swift, Drift, sqflite...). A file is a database when it starts with the SQLite header, its extension does not matter.
  • On every platform, only the listed databases can be queried.

docs.title: Setup
Registering databases
docs.text:
KotlinSwiftFlutter

Automatic detection. With room(), Flocon scans for SQLite database files: the app's databases folder on Android, Documents and Library on iOS. On JVM, give the folders to scan with room { path("/path/to/folder") }. Nothing is detected on Wasm.

Room databases (all platforms). To register a Room database (in-memory databases included) with a display name:

val dogDatabase = Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder(context, DogDatabase::class.java).build()

Flocon.databasePlugin.register(
    id = "inmemory_dogs",
    displayName = "In-Memory Dogs",
    database = dogDatabase,
)

The id is required, stable and unique: registering two different databases with the same id throws an IllegalArgumentException. It is the id the desktop app uses for everything on this database (browsing, queries, query logs), so the query logs of a database must be sent with the same id (see Query logging).

register(id, displayName, database) comes from io.github.openflocon.flocon.database.room (Room 2) or io.github.openflocon.flocon.database.room3 (Room 3).

SQLDelight databases. SQLDelight drivers are plain objects, so the database is registered through its driver. withFlocon registers it and shows its queries in the desktop app (see Query logging):

val driver = AndroidSqliteDriver(AppDatabase.Schema, context, "app.db")
    .withFlocon(id = "app", displayName = "App database") // io.github.openflocon.flocon.database.sqldelight.withFlocon
val database = AppDatabase(driver)

It works with every driver (AndroidSqliteDriver, JdbcSqliteDriver, NativeSqliteDriver) and needs install(FloconDatabase), with no provider: FloconDatabase itself is enough. Same rules on id as for Room. To only browse the database, without the query logs, use withFlocon(id, displayName, logQueries = false), or Flocon.databasePlugin.register(id, displayName, driver).

The SQL you run from the desktop app does not refresh the SQLDelight Flows of your app, and the column names of PRAGMA and EXPLAIN results are column_0, column_1... The web worker driver is not supported yet.

Room 3 on the web (Wasm). Room 3 runs on Wasm with WebWorkerSQLiteDriver (androidx.sqlite:sqlite-web), which talks to a SQLite Web Worker. There is no file system, so the databases are not discovered: register each Room database with register(id, displayName, database) (the plugin still has to be installed with install(FloconDatabase) { room() }):

val dogDatabase = Room.databaseBuilder<DogDatabase>(name = "dogs.db")
    .setDriver(WebWorkerSQLiteDriver(createWorker()))
    .build()

Flocon.databasePlugin.register(id = "dogs", displayName = "dogs", database = dogDatabase)

See FloconAndroid/sample/wasm in the repository for a complete setup (worker, npm package and KSP for wasmJs).

SQLite files (Kotlin Multiplatform). Any SQLite file can be registered with its absolute path:

Flocon.databasePlugin.register(
    FloconFileDatabaseModel(
        id = "app_db",
        displayName = "App DB",
        absolutePath = dbFile.absolutePath,
    )
)

Register a database that is not in Documents or Application Support, or give one a clearer name. Either at install time:

let url = URL.documentsDirectory.appending(path: "app.sqlite")

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.database) {
        $0.register(displayName: "App", url: url)
    }
}
#endif

or later, once the SDK is started:

Flocon.databasePlugin.register(displayName: "Shared", url: sharedDatabaseURL)
Flocon.databasePlugin.register(displayName: "Shared", absolutePath: "/path/to/shared.sqlite")

Registering a file that is already listed renames it. Databases found automatically are named after their path from their root, such as Documents/app.sqlite.

The id of a database is the absolute path of its file (FloconDatabase(displayName:url:).id), the same whatever the way the path is written.

Register a database stored elsewhere, or give one a clearer name:

import 'package:flocon/flocon.dart';
import 'package:flocon_database/flocon_database.dart';

Flocon.database.register('Shared', '/path/to/shared.sqlite');

The plugin must be installed first (the call does nothing before). A database already listed is renamed.

docs.title: Query logging
docs.text:
Flocon can display all SQL queries executed by your app in real time. It is great to verify the queries generated by Room or to detect slow multi-table joins.

KotlinSwiftFlutter

The queries run in the same transaction are grouped in one row, with the number of queries, the duration and whether the transaction was committed or rolled back. Click the row to show or hide its queries. Room 2 and Room 3 logging group them automatically, and the transactions nested in a transaction (savepoints) get a row of their own inside it, which you can fold too. A transaction of a single query is shown as a plain row. With manual logging, logQuery finds the transaction of a query from the BEGIN, SAVEPOINT, COMMIT... statements you log before it.

Room 2 (Android)Room 3SQLDelightManual Query Logging 
val database = Room.databaseBuilder(
    context.applicationContext,
    DogDatabase::class.java,
    "dogs_database"
)
    .floconLogs(id = "dogs") // io.github.openflocon.flocon.database.room.extensions.floconLogs
    .build()
    .also { Flocon.databasePlugin.register(id = "dogs", displayName = "dogs", database = it) }

The id given to floconLogs must be the one the database is registered with, otherwise the desktop app cannot show the queries with the database.

Room 3 has no query callback: wrap its SQLite driver instead.

Room.databaseBuilder<DogDatabase>(context, "dogs_database")
    .setDriver(AndroidSQLiteDriver().floconLogs(id = "dogs")) // io.github.openflocon.flocon.database.room3.floconLogs
    .build()
    .also { Flocon.databasePlugin.register(id = "dogs", displayName = "dogs", database = it) }

Wraps a synchronous driver (BundledSQLiteDriver, NativeSQLiteDriver, AndroidSQLiteDriver...), checked on Android with AndroidSQLiteDriver. Each statement is logged when it runs, with its arguments. Same rule as Room 2: the id is the one the database is registered with.

val driver = AndroidSqliteDriver(AppDatabase.Schema, context, "app.db")
    .floconLogs(id = "app") // io.github.openflocon.flocon.database.sqldelight.floconLogs

withFlocon does this and registers the database. Each query is logged once, when it is done, with its arguments (blobs are shown as their size). Failing queries are logged too. Unlike Room, the transactions are not grouped yet.

Flocon.databasePlugin.logQuery(
    dbId = "my_custom_db", // the id the database was registered with
    sqlQuery = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?",
    bindArgs = listOf(42),
)

Room only accepts one query callback per database. If your app already sets its own setQueryCallback, call logQuery from it to forward the queries to Flocon:

Room.databaseBuilder(context, DogDatabase::class.java, "dogs_database")
    .setQueryCallback({ sqlQuery, bindArgs ->
        Flocon.databasePlugin.logQuery("dogs", sqlQuery, bindArgs)
        myOwnLogger.log(sqlQuery)
    }, Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor())
    .build()

The SDK does not hook into Core Data, GRDB or SQLite.swift: call logQuery from the place where your app runs a statement (a trace callback, your own database wrapper...).

// by file location
Flocon.databasePlugin.logQuery(
    database: databaseURL,
    sqlQuery: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?",
    bindArgs: [42]
)

// or by id, the one of the registered database
Flocon.databasePlugin.logQuery(dbId: database.id, sqlQuery: "DELETE FROM users")

bindArgs is [Any?], a nil value is shown as null. The queries are linked to a database by its file, so they show up under it in the desktop app.

flocon_database browses and queries databases with sqflite, which has no query hook: log the queries from the hook of your database library. A query is linked to its database by the path of its file.

import 'package:flocon/flocon.dart';
import 'package:flocon_database/flocon_database.dart';

Flocon.database.logQuery(db.path, 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?', [42]);

For example with Drift, from a QueryInterceptor:

class FloconQueryInterceptor extends QueryInterceptor {
  FloconQueryInterceptor(this.path);
  final String path;

  @override
  Future<List<Map<String, Object?>>> runSelect(QueryExecutor e, String statement, List<Object?> args) {
    Flocon.database.logQuery(path, statement, args);
    return super.runSelect(e, statement, args);
  }
  // same for runInsert, runUpdate, runDelete, runCustom
}

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

Logged queries also show up in the Timeline, in the Database lane of the graph.

  • Sidebar: the databases of the app with their tables and columns (type, primary key, not null). Use the filter field to find a database, table or column, and double-click a table to open it.
  • SQL editor: write a query and run it, the result is shown as a table. Open several tabs, turn on auto-update to re-run a query regularly, copy the result or export it to CSV.
  • Row detail: select a row to see its values in full.
  • Saved queries: save a query as a favorite from the editor and run it again later.
  • Query logs: See all queries opens the queries your app ran on a database, newest first, with their arguments (you can copy the query or its arguments). The queries of a transaction are grouped in one row (count, duration, committed, rolled back or in progress).

Note

Queries from the desktop run on their own connection, next to the one of your app. With Flutter, blobs are shown in hexadecimal, truncated after 64 bytes.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_databases: the SQLite databases of the app, with the databaseId used by the other tools.
  • list_database_tables: the tables of a database with their columns, types and primary keys.
  • query_database: run a read-only SQL query (SELECT, PRAGMA without a value, EXPLAIN).
  • list_database_query_logs: the queries your app executed, newest first. Only available when the app logs its queries to Flocon (see Query logging).

Example prompts: "Show me the users table of the app database and tell me why two rows have the same email.", "Which queries did the app run when I opened the profile screen?"

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Kotlin: SQL run from the desktop does not refresh your SQLDelight Flows, and the web worker driver of SQLDelight is not supported.
  • Wasm: no SQLite files, only Room 3 with WebWorkerSQLiteDriver.
  • Swift and Flutter: queries are logged by hand, and transactions are not grouped.
  • The MCP tools only run read-only queries.

docs.title: 🔗 Deeplink Launcher
docs.text: Your app declares its deeplinks, with the parts to fill in ([userId]) and values shared between links ([host]). Flocon Desktop lists them, lets you fill the parameters with autocomplete, and opens the link on the device in one click. No more hand-written adb shell am start or xcrun simctl openurl commands.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Declare deeplinks, with parameters and variables ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Open a link from the desktop ✅ (adb) ✅ iOS Simulator only (simctl) ✅ iOS Simulator only (simctl) ✅ Android (adb), iOS Simulator
  • Android: the desktop runs adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "<link>" <your package>. It works on emulators and on real devices reachable with adb, and needs adb to be available on the desktop.
  • iOS Simulator: the desktop runs xcrun simctl openurl booted "<link>" (macOS with Xcode only). It targets the booted simulator.
  • Physical iOS devices are not supported: the links are listed, but the desktop cannot open them. Open the link from Safari or the Notes app on the device, or use xcrun simctl openurl on a simulator.
  • JVM / Wasm apps: the links are listed, but the Send button is disabled.
  • A desktop version that includes the iOS Simulator support is required (older versions only open links with adb).

docs.title: Setup
Parameters and variables
docs.text:
Write the parts to fill in between brackets: myapp://user/[userId]. Each part is one of:

  • A field you type each time, optionally with autocomplete suggestions (withAutoComplete in Kotlin, .autoComplete(name, suggestions) in Swift, FloconDeeplinkParameter.autoComplete(name, suggestions) in Flutter).
  • A variable: a value shared by several deeplinks ([host], a user id, an environment), edited once in the desktop (withVariable in Kotlin, .variable(name, variableName:) in Swift, FloconDeeplinkParameter.variable(name, variableName:) in Flutter).

A variable is either a free text input, or has a list of suggestions (autoComplete(...) in Kotlin, suggestions: in Swift and Flutter). A link that uses a variable without a value shows N required in the sidebar and cannot be sent.

label is the short name shown instead of the link, description says what it opens.

docs.title: Register deeplinks later
docs.text:
Some values are only known after Flocon starts (a user id after login, a feature enabled remotely...). Register more links at any time; the desktop is updated immediately and after each reconnection.

KotlinSwiftFlutter

register adds to the existing links: a deeplink with the same link, or a variable with the same name, replaces the previous one.

Flocon.deeplinksPlugin.register {
    variable("userId")

    deeplink("myapp://user/[userId]") {
        "userId" withVariable "userId"
    }
}

register replaces the whole list: pass every deeplink and variable you want to keep.

Flocon.deeplinksPlugin.register(
    deeplinks: [FloconDeeplink("myapp://user/[userId]", parameters: [.variable("userId", variableName: "userId")])],
    variables: [FloconDeeplinkVariable("userId")]
)

register replaces the whole list: pass every deeplink and variable you want to keep.

Flocon.deeplinks.register(
  [FloconDeeplink('myapp://user/[userId]', parameters: [FloconDeeplinkParameter.variable('userId', variableName: 'userId')])],
  variables: [FloconDeeplinkVariable('userId')],
);

docs.title: 🚩 Feature Flags Viewer
docs.text:
Flocon displays the feature flags evaluated by your app: for each flag, its provider, its variant and its optional payload. There is no dependency on a feature flag SDK: your app forwards the flags it already evaluated, from Firebase Remote Config, Statsig, LaunchDarkly, an in-house system...

For each flag the desktop shows:

  • Provider: where the flag comes from (for example firebase, statsig).
  • Name: the flag key.
  • State: On, Off or Custom (an experiment arm, a value...). The variant is colored with it, and each custom variant gets its own color.
  • Variant: the evaluated variant, a free string (for example control, treatment, on).
  • Payload: optional, often JSON, displayed formatted in the right panel when you click a flag.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Register flags per provider ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Change a flag from the desktop ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌

The viewer is read only on every platform: the desktop never sends a value back to the app. To try another variant, change it in your provider (or in your own code) and register the flags again.

docs.title: Setup
Usage
docs.text:
Register all the flags of a provider at once, one provider per feature flag system. Each call replaces the flags previously sent for this provider, and they are sent again automatically when the app reconnects to the desktop.

state tells the desktop how to color the variant: on, off, or custom for an experiment arm or a value.

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.Flocon
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.featureflags.featureFlagsPlugin
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.featureflags.model.FloconFeatureFlag
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.featureflags.model.FloconFeatureFlagState

Flocon.featureFlagsPlugin.register(
    provider = "firebase",
    FloconFeatureFlag(name = "new_checkout", state = FloconFeatureFlagState.Custom, variant = "treatment", payload = """{"buttonColor":"#FF5722"}"""),
    FloconFeatureFlag(name = "dark_mode", state = FloconFeatureFlagState.On, variant = "on"),
    FloconFeatureFlag(name = "onboarding_v2", state = FloconFeatureFlagState.Off, variant = "control"),
)

register also takes a List<FloconFeatureFlag>.

Flocon.featureFlagsPlugin.sender("firebase").register(
    FloconFeatureFlag(name: "new_checkout", state: .custom, variant: "treatment", payload: #"{"steps": 3}"#),
    FloconFeatureFlag(name: "dark_mode", state: .on, variant: "on"),
    FloconFeatureFlag(name: "onboarding_v2", state: .off, variant: "control")
)

register also takes an array. Keep the sender (let firebase = Flocon.featureFlagsPlugin.sender("firebase")) to reuse it.

Flocon.featureFlags.register('firebase', [
  FloconFeatureFlag(name: 'new_checkout', state: FloconFeatureFlagState.custom, variant: 'treatment', payload: '{"steps": 3}'),
  FloconFeatureFlag(name: 'dark_mode', state: FloconFeatureFlagState.on, variant: 'on'),
  FloconFeatureFlag(name: 'onboarding_v2', state: FloconFeatureFlagState.off, variant: 'control'),
]);

docs.title: Generic feature flags forwarder
docs.text:
Forward your flags to Flocon each time your provider refreshes them:

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
class FeatureFlagsRepository(private val remoteConfig: FirebaseRemoteConfig) {

    fun onFlagsActivated() {
        Flocon.featureFlagsPlugin.register(
            provider = "firebase",
            flags = remoteConfig.all.map { (key, value) ->
                FloconFeatureFlag(
                    name = key,
                    state = when (value.asString()) {
                        "true" -> FloconFeatureFlagState.On
                        "false" -> FloconFeatureFlagState.Off
                        else -> FloconFeatureFlagState.Custom
                    },
                    variant = value.asString(),
                )
            },
        )
    }
}

func onFlagsRefreshed(_ values: [String: String]) {
    Flocon.featureFlagsPlugin.sender("remote_config").register(
        values.map { key, value in
            FloconFeatureFlag(
                name: key,
                state: value == "true" ? .on : value == "false" ? .off : .custom,
                variant: value
            )
        }
    )
}

void onFlagsRefreshed(Map<String, String> values) {
  Flocon.featureFlags.register('remote_config', [
    for (final entry in values.entries)
      FloconFeatureFlag(
        name: entry.key,
        state: switch (entry.value) {
          'true' => FloconFeatureFlagState.on,
          'false' => FloconFeatureFlagState.off,
          _ => FloconFeatureFlagState.custom,
        },
        variant: entry.value,
      ),
  ]);
}

  • Click a flag to see its state, variant and payload (formatted when it is JSON) in the right panel, where the payload can be copied.

docs.title: 📁 Sandbox File Explorer
docs.text: Flocon lets you explore the sandboxed storage of your app (files, caches, exports, logs, database files) from the desktop, without ADB shell commands or Xcode container downloads. You can open a file, copy its path, download it and delete files or the content of a folder.

docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Browse, download, delete ✅ ✅ (iOS, JVM; no Wasm) ✅ ✅ Default folders ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Register your own folder ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ App Group container n/a ✅ (iOS) ✅ ❌ Platform Folders shown without registering anything Android Files (filesDir), Caches (cacheDir), Databases iOS (Kotlin) Documents, Application Support, Caches, tmp, App container JVM (Kotlin) Working directory, Temp, Home Swift Documents, Application Support, Caches, tmp, App container Flutter Documents, Application Support, Caches, tmp, and on Android and iOS the whole App container (on macOS only inside the sandbox)

Wasm

Showing another folder
In Flocon Desktop

docs.title: 🛰️ GraphQL
docs.text: Flocon recognises GraphQL calls among your HTTP traffic and shows them with their operation type and query, next to the usual headers, bodies and timings. There is nothing GraphQL-specific to install: if your GraphQL client goes through a network interceptor, its calls are captured.

docs.title: How Flocon detects GraphQL
docs.text:
Detection happens in the desktop app, from the HTTP request, on every platform. A call is a GraphQL call when:

  • its body is a JSON object with a query field (the standard { "query": "...", "variables": {...} } POST) containing a query, mutation or subscription operation; or
  • its URL has an operationName and an extensions query parameter containing persistedQuery (a persisted query sent with GET). It is shown as a persistedQuery operation.

Anything else stays a regular HTTP call.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter GraphQL detection ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

The detection does not depend on the SDK, only on the shape of the request. What changes is which client you plug Flocon into.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use the network setup of the HTTP client your GraphQL library relies on.

KotlinSwiftFlutter

Apollo Kotlin on Android and JVM delegates its calls to OkHttp. Give it an OkHttpClient with the Flocon interceptor:

val okHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(FloconOkhttpInterceptor())
    .build()

val apolloClient = ApolloClient.Builder()
    .serverUrl("https://your-api.com/graphql")
    .okHttpClient(okHttpClient)
    .build()

okHttpClient(...) is the Apollo extension from com.apollographql.apollo.network.okHttpClient. Do not forget install(FloconNetwork) when you start Flocon.

Any GraphQL client that sends its requests with URLSession is captured once its session uses a Flocon configuration:

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { $0.install(.network) }
#endif

let session = URLSession(configuration: .default.withFlocon())

Hand session (or the configuration) to the GraphQL client, if it lets you choose one. The calls made with URLSession.shared are captured by install(.network) alone.

Use a Dio or package:http client wrapped with Flocon, and give it to your GraphQL client:

final client = http.Client().withFlocon();   // flocon_http

With graphql_flutter, pass it to the link: HttpLink('https://api.example.com/graphql', httpClient: client).

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

GraphQL calls also show up in the Timeline, like any network call.

GraphQL calls are listed in the Network screen, tagged with their operation (query, mutation, ...), and open in the usual detail panel with an extra GraphQl section:

  • the query, its type and its status;
  • the formatted request body, with the variables, and the formatted response;
  • the HTTP headers, status code, duration and size;
  • the Export GraphQl as image action, to share the section.

Status of a GraphQL call

The GraphQL status follows the HTTP status code (success for 2xx). A GraphQL response that returns an errors array with a 200 is shown as a success: read the response body to see the errors.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
GraphQL calls come through the network tools, with their type and query:

  • list_network_calls: use the type filter to keep GraphQL calls.
  • get_network_call: returns the GraphQL query and the response.
  • search_network_calls: finds a query by its name.

"Which GraphQL mutation failed in the last session, and with what variables?"

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Calls made with a GraphQL client that does not use an intercepted HTTP client are not captured.
  • GraphQL over WebSocket (subscriptions) is a WebSocket connection: see WebSockets.

docs.title: ⚡ gRPC
docs.text:
Flocon logs your gRPC calls in the Network screen: the server, the method, the request and response messages as JSON, the metadata, the duration and the gRPC status. It saves you from decoding Protocol Buffers by hand.

For each call you see:

  • the server as the URL, and the full method name (helloworld.Greeter/SayHello);
  • the request and response messages, serialised as JSON;
  • the metadata (headers), the duration and the gRPC status (OK, NOT_FOUND...);
  • the error, such as a refused connection, when the call fails.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Inspect gRPC calls ✅ grpc-java / grpc-android ❌ ✅ grpc-swift 1.x ❌ Bad network simulation ✅ latency and exceptions ❌ ❌ ❌ Mocks ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌

Not available in the Flutter SDK yet

Flutter has no gRPC interceptor. Only HTTP calls (Dio, package:http) and WebSocket events are reported.

Not available in Kotlin Multiplatform yet

The gRPC interceptors are Android only (grpc-java). On iOS, use the Swift SDK with grpc-swift.

docs.title: Setup
Usage
In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

gRPC calls also show up in the Timeline, like any network call.

gRPC calls are listed with the other calls in the Network screen. Their URL is the server, their method is the full method name, and their status is the gRPC status (OK, NOT_FOUND...). Click a call to see its metadata and its request and response messages as formatted JSON.

The bad network simulation applies to gRPC calls on Android. Mocks do not.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
gRPC calls come through the network tools, with their status:

  • list_network_calls: filter on the gRPC type, or on errors only (a status other than OK).
  • get_network_call: returns the metadata, the JSON messages and the gRPC status.

"List the gRPC calls that failed with a status other than OK and show me the request of the first one."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Android (grpc-java) and iOS / macOS (grpc-swift 1.x) only. No Kotlin Multiplatform, no Flutter.
  • gRPC calls cannot be mocked.
  • On Swift, a streaming call shows only its first request message and its last response message.
  • The Swift SDK does not apply the bad network simulation to gRPC.

docs.title: 🖼️ Images
docs.text:
Flocon collects the images your app downloads (avatars, feed thumbnails, banners, media) in a gallery. It helps you debug a missing placeholder, a CDN that resolves wrong, an image that is too heavy, or a cache that does not cache.

There is no separate plugin for images. An image is a network call whose response is flagged as an image: Flocon does not send the image bytes, it sends the call, and the desktop app downloads the image from its URL to display it.

The URL must be reachable from your computer

Since the desktop fetches the image itself, an image behind a private network, a short-lived signed URL or a header only your app can send will not show up as a picture. The call is still listed.

docs.title: How an image is detected
docs.text:
A response is an image when:

  • its Content-Type starts with image/ (automatic, on every SDK), or
  • your isImage option returns true for it. Use it for CDNs that answer with application/octet-stream or without a content type.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter image/* detection ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ isImage predicate ✅ OkHttp, Ktor ✅ Ktor (and OkHttp on JVM) ✅ FloconNetworkOptions ✅ FloconNetwork

Images are captured through the network interceptors, so an image loader is covered only when it uses an intercepted HTTP client (OkHttp or Ktor, a URLSession with withFlocon(), a Dio or http client).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Follow the network setup. Then make your image loader use the intercepted HTTP client.

KotlinSwiftFlutter

With Coil 3, give the ImageLoader the client that has the Flocon interceptor.

OkHttpKtor 
SingletonImageLoader.setSafe {
    ImageLoader.Builder(context = context)
        .components {
            add(
                OkHttpNetworkFetcherFactory(
                    callFactory = { okHttpClient }, // built with FloconOkhttpInterceptor
                )
            )
        }
        .build()
}

OkHttpNetworkFetcherFactory comes from io.coil-kt.coil3:coil-network-okhttp.

SingletonImageLoader.setSafe {
    ImageLoader.Builder(context = context)
        .components {
            add(KtorNetworkFetcherFactory(httpClient)) // built with FloconKtorPlugin
        }
        .build()
}

KtorNetworkFetcherFactory comes from io.coil-kt.coil3:coil-network-ktor3.

Make your image downloader use a Flocon session configuration. Kingfisher, for example:

KingfisherManager.shared.downloader.sessionConfiguration = .default.withFlocon()

Images loaded through URLSession.shared are captured by install(.network).

To flag more images than Content-Type: image/*:

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.network) { options in
        options.isImage = { request, _ in request.url?.path.hasPrefix("/images/") == true }
    }
}
#endif

Load your images through a flocon_http or flocon_dio client. Responses with an image/* type are flagged automatically. To flag more:

await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon
  ..install(FloconNetwork(
    isImage: (request, response) => request.url.host == 'images.example.com',
  )));

Image.network and the image packages that use their own HTTP client are not captured.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: Nothing to call: images appear in the Images screen as your app loads them.

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
Open the Images screen.

  • Gallery: switch between a grid and a list. Each image shows its thumbnail, URL, size, weight, format and load time.
  • Filter: type in Filter images to keep the URLs that match.
  • Viewer: click an image to open it large. Zoom in, Zoom out, Fit to window, move with the previous and next arrows or the filmstrip, and close it with Close.
  • Actions: Copy URL, Open in browser and Download image save the file to your computer.
  • Clear images: empties the gallery.

The call of an image is also in the Network screen, flagged as an image response, with its headers and timings.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_images: lists the images loaded by the app (URL and load time, newest first), with a text filter. It does not return the image content.

"List the images loaded on the home screen and tell me which hosts serve them."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The image bytes are not sent by the app: the desktop downloads them from the URL.
  • Only images loaded by an intercepted HTTP client are listed.

docs.title: Flutter SDK
docs.text:
Requirements: Dart 3.10 / Flutter 3.38.1 or later. Android, iOS and macOS are supported.

Let your AI agent do it

The Flocon plugin adds the packages, starts Flocon and keeps it out of release builds for you.

docs.title: 1. Add the packages
docs.text:
flutter pub add flocon

Then add only the packages you need:

Platform setup (see sample/ in the repository for a working configuration):

  • Android: the INTERNET permission in AndroidManifest.xml.
  • iOS: NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription in Info.plist, so the app can reach your computer on the local network.
  • macOS: the com.apple.security.network.client entitlement.

No cleartext or App Transport Security exception is needed: the SDK uses wss:// and https:// with the self-signed certificate of the desktop (encrypted, not authenticated).

docs.title: 2. Start Flocon
docs.text:
Start the SDK as early as possible, then install the features you use. A feature that is not installed does nothing instead of crashing, so calls to it can stay in your code.

import 'package:flocon/flocon.dart';
import 'package:flocon_database/flocon_database.dart';
import 'package:flocon_shared_preferences/flocon_shared_preferences.dart';
import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';
import 'package:shared_preferences/shared_preferences.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  if (kDebugMode) await initializeFlocon(); // debug builds only
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

Future<void> initializeFlocon() async {
  final prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance();
  await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon
    ..install(FloconNetwork())
    ..install(FloconDatabase())
    ..install(FloconSharedPreferences(prefs)));
}

The plugins of the flocon package (network, analytics, tables, timeline, feature flags, deeplinks, dashboard) are always available through Flocon.analytics, Flocon.timeline, ...; install FloconNetwork only to give it options. The plugins of the other packages must be installed: FloconDatabase, FloconSharedPreferences, FloconFiles, FloconCrashReporter. Calling startFlocon more than once has no effect. Flocon.isLoggingEnabled = true, set before starting, prints what the SDK does.

docs.title: Release builds
docs.text:
Flocon is a debugging tool: once connected, the desktop can read your network calls, edit your preferences, delete files and run SQL on your databases. Keep it out of release builds.

Start Flocon only in debug builds with kDebugMode (a constant, removed from release builds by the compiler). Every other Flocon call (Flocon.analytics, withFlocon()...) does nothing when Flocon was not started. Use !kReleaseMode to also keep profile builds.

The packages stay in your dependencies, so their native code is still in the release binary. To keep the Flocon Dart code out of it too, start Flocon from a debug-only entry point and keep every Flocon import there:

// lib/main_debug.dart
import 'package:flocon/flocon.dart';
import 'package:flutter/widgets.dart';
import 'main.dart' as app;

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon..install(FloconNetwork()));
  app.main();
}

flutter run -t lib/main_debug.dart   # debug, with Flocon
flutter build apk                    # release, from lib/main.dart, without Flocon
