docs.title: The two skills
docs.text:
The Flocon plugin (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) also installs two skills: short instructions your agent loads when relevant.

Skill What it does flocon-mcp Teaches the agent how to debug with Flocon: which tool to use for what (start with get_timeline, then the detail tools), how targeting works, what to say when a call fails (Desktop not running, no device connected, unknown app), what each SDK sends, and the rules: prefer disabling a mock over deleting it, always turn bad network off, ask before editing a preference, tell you everything it changed. flocon-setup Installs Flocon in an existing project, or migrates it from 1.x to 2.0. It detects the platform (Android, Kotlin Multiplatform, Swift, Flutter), adds the dependencies, keeps Flocon out of release builds, installs only the plugins the project really uses, and checks that each feature is captured. See the Cookbook.

Without the plugin, the MCP server alone works too: the server sends its own usage instructions to the agent.

docs.title: A few examples
docs.text:
Just ask your agent in plain text.

"My article page doesn't display, is it caused by a network call?" The agent lists the failed calls, opens the one for the article, and tells you that GET /articles/42 returned a 500. See Why does this request fail.

"Make the articles endpoint fail with a 500 so I can check my error screen." The agent creates a mock from a real call, changes only the status code, and offers to disable it afterwards. See Mock an endpoint.

"What happened in the app just before it crashed?" The agent reads the timeline around the latest crash: a loop of calls, a 401, an analytics event two seconds before. See Crash triage.

docs.title: Testing the server
docs.text:
You can browse the tools with the MCP Inspector:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector

Then connect to http://localhost:9042/mcp with the Streamable HTTP transport. The Tools tab lists the 57 tools and lets you call them by hand.

docs.title: Port 9042
docs.text:
The MCP server always uses port 9042: it cannot be changed from Flocon. This is not the port your apps use: they connect to Flocon Desktop on the websocket port (default 9023) and HTTP port (default 9024). Those two can be changed in the Flocon settings, or by an agent with set_server_ports. Port 9042 is reserved, so you cannot use it for them.

Port already used

If port 9042 is already used by another program, Flocon Desktop displays an error and retries every 10 seconds. Close the other program: the server starts by itself once the port is free.

If your agent says it cannot connect, check that Flocon Desktop is running, then see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: 🧭 Migrating from 1.x to 2.0
docs.text:
Swift and Flutter SDKs

This guide is for the Kotlin SDK, the only one that had a 1.x. The Swift SDK (FloconSwift) and the Flutter SDK (FloconFlutter, packages flocon, flocon_dio...) were published as 0.x pre-releases and are aligned on 2.0.0 with the desktop and the Kotlin SDK. There is nothing to migrate if you start with them, see Getting started. If you used a 0.x version, update to 2.0.0 (the Flutter changelog lists no user-facing change for 2.0.0; the Swift SDK has no changelog) and keep the SDK and the desktop on the same major version.

Flocon 2.0 splits the SDK into one module per feature: you only add what you use, and every module has a -no-op twin for release builds. The SDK is now initialized with a small DSL where you install the plugins you need, and every plugin is reached the same way: Flocon.xxxPlugin.

docs.title: 1. Dependencies
docs.text:
In 1.x, io.github.openflocon:flocon contained every feature. In 2.0, flocon is the core (connection to the desktop app + dashboards) and each feature has its own artifact:

Feature Artifact Platforms Core + Dashboards flocon Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm Network (mocks, bad network) flocon-network-core Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm OkHttp interceptor + WebSockets flocon-okhttp-interceptor Android, JVM Ktor plugin flocon-ktor-interceptor Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm gRPC interceptor flocon-grpc-interceptor / flocon-grpc-interceptor-lite (+ flocon-grpc-interceptor-base) Android Databases flocon-database-core + flocon-database-room (Room 2), flocon-database-room3 (Room 3) or flocon-database-sqldelight Android, JVM, iOS (+ Wasm for Room 3) SharedPreferences / custom stores flocon-sharedprefs Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm DataStore flocon-datastores Android, JVM, iOS Analytics flocon-analytics Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm Feature flags flocon-feature-flags Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm Tables flocon-tables Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm Deeplinks flocon-deeplinks Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm Files flocon-files Android, JVM, iOS (Wasm: no file browsing) Crash reporter flocon-crashreporter Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm Timeline flocon-timeline Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm Accessibility flocon-accessibility Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm WebView flocon-webview Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm QR code scanner flocon-qr-scanner Android

flocon-base is gone

The 1.x flocon-base artifact no longer exists. Code that logged WebSocket events or database queries from a module compiled in every variant must now depend on flocon-network-core / flocon-database-core in debug and on their -no-op in release.

Every artifact has a -no-op version with the same API (e.g. flocon-analytics-no-op). See Release builds.

docs.title: Platform support details
docs.text:
• Wasm: connects to the desktop app (WebSocket) but has no filesystem or SQLite, so files, databases and crash persistence are not available.
  • iOS: files, crash reporter (stored in Application Support), network mock persistence, UserDefaults preferences and the app icon work. Databases are searched in Documents/Library, or in the folders given with path(...).
  • JVM: Room databases are found in the folders given with room { path("...") }.

docs.title: 2. Initialization
3. API mapping
docs.text:
Every plugin is now accessed with Flocon.xxxPlugin:

1.x 2.0 Flocon.initialize(context) startFlocon(FloconContext(context)) { install(...) } Flocon.deeplinks { ... } install(FloconDeeplinks) { ... } floconAnalytics("stream").logEvents(event) Flocon.analyticsPlugin.log(AnalyticsEvent("name", "stream", ...)) floconTable("name").log("key" toParam "value") Flocon.tablePlugin.table("name") { column("key", "value") } floconDashboard(id) { ... } Flocon.dashboardPlugin.dashboard(id, scope) { ... } floconRegisterPreference(preference) Flocon.preferencesPlugin.register(preference) floconRegisterDatabase(...) Flocon.databasePlugin.register("id", "name", roomDatabase) (the id is required and unique) floconLogDatabaseQuery(...) Flocon.databasePlugin.logQuery(dbId, ...) or RoomDatabase.Builder.floconLogs(id), with the id the database is registered with floconLogWebSocketEvent(event) Flocon.networkPlugin.logWebSocket(event) Flocon.deeplinks { ... } (registered later) Flocon.deeplinksPlugin.register { ... } Flocon.analytics("table").logEvents(event) Flocon.analyticsPlugin.log(AnalyticsEvent(name, "table", props)) or .sender("table").log(...)

Packages moved with the modules, for example io.github.openflocon.flocon.plugins.network.model.FloconWebSocketEvent became io.github.openflocon.flocon.network.core.model.FloconWebSocketEvent, and ...plugins.analytics.model.* became ...analytics.model.*. Fix the imports after changing the dependencies.

The accessors are: analyticsPlugin, crashReporterPlugin, dashboardPlugin, databasePlugin, deeplinksPlugin, featureFlagsPlugin, filesPlugin, networkPlugin, preferencesPlugin and tablePlugin, timelinePlugin, webViewPlugin and accessibilityPlugin (plus databaseRoom / databaseRoom3 for the Room providers).

docs.title: 4. Behavior changes
docs.text:
• Crash reporter: crashes are captured as soon as FloconCrashReporter is installed (catchFatalErrors = true by default) and sent to the desktop app on the next connection.
  • Interceptors without Flocon: the OkHttp, Ktor and gRPC interceptors let the calls go through untouched when FloconNetwork is not installed.
  • Desktop menu: when it connects, the SDK tells the desktop app which plugins are installed. The desktop only shows the menu items of the installed plugins (an older SDK that does not send them shows everything). Sections can be collapsed, and items can be pinned (pin icon on hover) to stay at the top.
  • Encrypted connection: the SDK connects to the desktop with wss:// / https:// instead of ws:// / http://. The desktop no longer serves the plain ports, so update the SDK and Flocon Desktop together (an old SDK cannot connect to a new desktop, and the other way around). The desktop certificate is self-signed and is not verified by the SDK: the connection is encrypted, not authenticated. The cleartext rule for localhost / 127.0.0.1 (and the one flocon-connect used to add for any IP address) is no longer needed, you can remove it from your network_security_config.xml.
  • Preference type: FloconPreference has a new type property, shown next to the preference name in the desktop app. It defaults to "Custom" in Kotlin; a Swift class implementing the Kotlin FloconPreference interface through the KMP framework must declare it (Kotlin default values are not visible from Swift).
  • Release builds now use flocon-no-op + one no-op per plugin: nothing is started and no connection is made to the desktop app.

docs.title: 5. Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A plugin must be installed. Flocon.dashboardPlugin.dashboard(...) compiles without install(FloconDashboard) but does nothing at runtime. After migrating, list every Flocon.xxxPlugin you call and check each one is installed.
  • Name clashes. FloconDashboard, FloconNetwork... are now objects of the SDK. If your project has a class with the same name, import the SDK one with an alias (import ...FloconDashboard as FloconDashboardPlugin).
  • Code compiled in every variant. A call to a plugin from main needs the real module in debug and its -no-op in release (and in any other non-debug variant, e.g. an internal distribution build).
  • Databases need a provider. install(FloconDatabase) alone discovers nothing: add the Room provider with install(FloconDatabase) { room() } (and the flocon-database-room or -room3 dependency). On Android it then scans the app databases folder; Flocon.databasePlugin.register(id, name, db) is only needed for in-memory databases or a custom name. logQuery takes the id of the database as the desktop lists it.
  • No Device plugin. The app icon is sent by the core, nothing to install. The flocon-device module and the "restart the app" action of the desktop no longer exist: remove flocon-device and install(FloconDevice) if the project has them.
  • Cleartext rules. The localhost / 127.0.0.1 cleartext exceptions in network_security_config.xml are no longer needed.
  • Gradle task names differ per module (flavors or not). List them with ./gradlew :module:tasks --all before building.

docs.title: 6. Migrating with an AI agent
docs.text: The flocon-setup skill of the Flocon plugin follows this guide: it detects the 1.x usage, picks the modules, updates the dependencies and the no-ops, rewrites the initialization and compiles. See MCP for the plugin install.

docs.title: 🎭 Mocking
docs.text:
Flocon lets you intercept a live HTTP call and answer it with a response you wrote, from the desktop app. Test a 401, a 404 or a 500, feed your screen a JSON from an unreleased backend, or add a delay to see your loaders, all without editing your code or redeploying.

You can:

  • Simulate errors: return 401, 404, 429 or 500 and check your error handling.
  • Inject a payload: answer with any JSON body, headers and status code.
  • Throw an exception: simulate a dropped connection (IOException, timeout) instead of a response.
  • Add a delay: slow the mocked response down.
  • Clone a real call: turn a captured call into a mock in one click.

Mocks are applied by the network interceptors. To degrade the real network instead of replacing responses, see Bad Network Simulation.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter HTTP mocks ✅ OkHttp, Ktor ✅ Ktor (and OkHttp on JVM) ✅ URLSession ✅ Dio, package:http gRPC mocks ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌ WebSocket message injection ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌
  • The mocks are saved on the device and apply from the next launch too, before the app reconnects to the desktop (on every SDK).
  • gRPC calls cannot be mocked, on any platform. See gRPC.
  • A WebSocket cannot be mocked, but on Android you can inject a message into a connection. See WebSockets.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Mocking needs nothing more than the network setup: install the network plugin and attach the interceptor of your HTTP client. Mocks are then applied automatically.

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
startFlocon(FloconContext(context)) {
    install(FloconNetwork)
}
OkHttpKtor 
val okHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(FloconOkhttpInterceptor())
    .build()

val httpClient = HttpClient {
    install(FloconKtorPlugin)
}

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.network)
}
#endif

let session = URLSession(configuration: .default.withFlocon())

The mocks apply to URLSession.shared and to the sessions created with withFlocon(). A request excluded by shouldLog is neither logged nor mocked.

await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon..install(FloconNetwork()));

final dio = Dio().withFlocon();             // flocon_dio
final client = http.Client().withFlocon();  // flocon_http

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
The mocks are managed from the desktop: follow the steps below.

How a request is matched

A mock has a URL pattern, which is a regular expression that must match the whole URL, and an HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, or * for all). The first matching mock answers the call.

Example: https://api.example.com/users/.* matches every user URL.

docs.title: Step 1: Install the network interceptor
docs.text: Follow the Setup above, then run your app.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect the app to Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
1. Launch your app on an emulator, a simulator or a physical device.
  2. Open Flocon Desktop.
  3. Check that your device and package name appear in the top-left device selector.

docs.title: Step 3: Trigger a baseline call
docs.text:
1. In your app, do something that makes a network call (load a profile, fetch items).
  2. In Flocon Desktop, open the Network tab.
  3. The call appears in the list with its method, URL, status code and duration.

docs.title: Step 4: Open the Mocks manager
docs.text:
Two ways in:

  • From the toolbar: click the Mocks icon in the toolbar of the Network tab. The manager lists your mocks and lets you add one.
  • From a captured call (recommended): select the call, then click Create Mock in the detail panel. The editor opens with the URL, the method, the headers and the original response body already filled in.

docs.title: Step 5: Write the mock
docs.text:
In the editor:

  1. Expectation
    • URL Pattern (Regex): the pattern to match. The Test URL Pattern field tells you whether a URL matches.
    • Method: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH or *.
  2. Response, choose a type:
    • HttpCode + Body: the HTTP Code (200, 401, 404, 500...), the Media Type, the Headers and the Body, with JSON highlighting.
    • Exception: throw an exception instead of answering, to simulate a failed connection (see below).
  3. Additional Delay (ms): wait before answering (for example 1500) to see loading states.
  4. Display name, and Shared across apps & devices if the mock must apply to every app, not only this one.
  5. Save.

docs.title: Step 6: Trigger the call again
docs.text:
1. Go back to your app and repeat the action (pull to refresh, reopen the screen).
  2. In the app: it receives the mocked response without reaching the server.
  3. In Flocon Desktop: the call is in the Network list with a MOCK tag.

docs.title: Step 7: Manage your mocks
docs.text:
In the Mocks manager:

  • Enable and disable: each mock has a switch, so you can turn it off without losing it.
  • Simulate a hard failure: choose the Exception type and select a class (SocketTimeoutException, UnknownHostException, ConnectException, SSLHandshakeException, IOException) to test your retry and offline states.
  • Export and import: save your mocks to a file and import them back. Share a suite with your team, attach edge cases to a bug report, or switch between profiles (happy path, outage...).

On Swift and Flutter, the exception class of the desktop is turned into the closest native error (URLError on Swift, a DioException on Dio): a timeout class gives a timeout, a connection class a connection error.

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
Everything above happens in the Network screen:

  • the Mocks toolbar button opens the manager (list, switches, export, import);
  • Create Mock in the call detail starts from a real call;
  • mocked calls are tagged MOCK in the list.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_network_mocks, get_network_mock: read the mocks.
  • create_network_mock: creates a mock, optionally from a captured call (fromCallId) with only the fields to override (for example the status code).
  • update_network_mock: edits a mock, and enables or disables it.
  • delete_network_mock: removes a mock.

"Mock the /profile call with a 500 error, then reload the screen and tell me what the app displays."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Step Where 1. Install install(FloconNetwork) plus the interceptor, install(.network) plus withFlocon(), or withFlocon() on Dio / http 2. Connect The device appears in the top bar of Flocon Desktop 3. Capture Trigger a call from the app 4. Open Mocks toolbar button, or Create Mock on a call 5. Write URL regex, method, status, body, delay 6. Verify Repeat the call and look for the MOCK tag

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• gRPC calls cannot be mocked.
  • WebSocket frames cannot be mocked. Only Android can inject a message into a connection.
  • Requests excluded by your shouldLog option are never mocked.

docs.title: 📡 Network
docs.text:
Flocon captures the HTTP calls your app makes and lists them live in the desktop app: method, URL, status, duration, size, headers and bodies. You see what your app really sends and receives, without a proxy or a certificate to install.

For every call, Flocon shows:

  • Method and URL: the HTTP method and the full URL, with the query parameters split out.
  • Headers and body: request and response, with a JSON viewer, search and copy.
  • Metrics: status code, duration, payload size and timestamp.
  • Errors: connection drops, timeouts and failed calls, with the error message.

The same capture also feeds Mocking, Bad Network Simulation, GraphQL, WebSockets, gRPC and Images.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter HTTP capture ✅ OkHttp, Ktor ✅ Ktor (and OkHttp on JVM) ✅ URLSession ✅ Dio, package:http Mocks ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Bad network simulation ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ shouldLog / isImage options ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
  • OkHttp works on Android and JVM. Ktor works on every Kotlin target: Android, iOS, JVM and Wasm (Ktor 3.x).
  • On Swift, anything built on URLSession is captured once its configuration goes through withFlocon() (Alamofire, Kingfisher, ...).
  • On Flutter, the flocon_dio and flocon_http packages add the capture. Other HTTP clients are not covered.
  • gRPC and WebSockets have their own pages: gRPC, WebSockets.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The network plugin is the one that talks to the desktop. The interceptors only report to it: without the plugin, they let your calls go through untouched.

KotlinSwiftFlutter

Add flocon-network-core and the interceptor of your HTTP client. Use the real modules in debug and the -no-op ones in release (see Release builds).

OkHttpKtor 
dependencies {
    debugImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core:LAST_VERSION")
    releaseImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core-no-op:LAST_VERSION")
    debugImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-okhttp-interceptor:LAST_VERSION")
    releaseImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-okhttp-interceptor-no-op:LAST_VERSION")
}

With a version catalog:

[libraries]
flocon-network = { module = "io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core", version.ref = "flocon" }
flocon-network-no-op = { module = "io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core-no-op", version.ref = "flocon" }
flocon-okhttp = { module = "io.github.openflocon:flocon-okhttp-interceptor", version.ref = "flocon" }
flocon-okhttp-no-op = { module = "io.github.openflocon:flocon-okhttp-interceptor-no-op", version.ref = "flocon" }

kotlin {
    sourceSets {
        commonMain.dependencies {
            implementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core:LAST_VERSION")
            implementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-ktor-interceptor:LAST_VERSION")
        }
    }
}

With a version catalog:

[libraries]
flocon-network = { module = "io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core", version.ref = "flocon" }
flocon-network-no-op = { module = "io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core-no-op", version.ref = "flocon" }
flocon-ktor = { module = "io.github.openflocon:flocon-ktor-interceptor", version.ref = "flocon" }
flocon-ktor-no-op = { module = "io.github.openflocon:flocon-ktor-interceptor-no-op", version.ref = "flocon" }

Then install the plugin when you start Flocon:

startFlocon(FloconContext(context)) {
    install(FloconNetwork)
}

Add the package https://github.com/openflocon/FloconSwift.git (from: "LAST_VERSION", product Flocon), then install the network feature:

import Flocon

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.network)
}
#endif

install(.network) also intercepts URLSession.shared. Sessions created with their own configuration need withFlocon() (see Usage).

flutter pub add flocon flocon_dio flocon_http

Add only the package of the HTTP client you use (flocon_dio for Dio, flocon_http for package:http). FloconNetwork is optional: install it only to set options.

import 'package:flocon/flocon.dart';
import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  if (kDebugMode) {
    await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon..install(FloconNetwork()));
  }
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

docs.title: Usage
In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

Each call also shows up in the Timeline: a request line and a response line in the list, a bar in the graph.

Open the Network screen. Calls appear as they are made, with their state (waiting, success, error).

  • List: columns for time, method, host, request and status, plus the duration. Use the filter box to search, and include or exclude a value from the context menu of a cell (host, method, request, status). Auto scroll follows new calls and Invert list puts the newest first.
  • Sessions: only the current app session is shown. Turn on Display old sessions to see earlier launches, and clear old sessions when the list gets long.
  • Deep Search: searches inside the headers and bodies of the calls.
  • Detail panel: click a call to see its request and response headers, bodies, query parameters, sizes and timings. You can pin the panel, open it in its own window, and decode the Authorization JWT.
  • Body viewer: JSON bodies are formatted and searchable. Open one in full screen, or Diff two bodies.
  • Actions on a call: Copy cURL, Copy URL, Replay the request, Create Mock from the call, and share it as Markdown, HTML or an image.
  • Selection: select several calls to act on them together.
  • Import / export: export the list to CSV, and import a CSV back.
  • Mocks and Bad network: two toolbar buttons open the Mocks and Bad Network Simulation managers.

A call answered by a mock carries a MOCK tag.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_network_calls: lists the captured calls, newest first, with filters (URL, method, status code, errors only, type).
  • search_network_calls: searches a text in URLs, headers and bodies, including old sessions.
  • get_network_call: returns the full detail of a call, with the equivalent cURL command.

"Find the failed calls since the last launch and tell me which endpoint returns the 500."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: 🚀 Getting started
docs.text:
Flocon has two parts:

  1. Flocon Desktop: the app on your computer where you inspect and control your running app.
  2. A Flocon SDK, added to your app in debug builds: Kotlin (Android and Kotlin Multiplatform), Swift (iOS and macOS) or Flutter (Android, iOS and macOS).

Three steps, a few minutes.

Coming from 1.x?

Only the Kotlin SDK existed before 2.0. See the migration guide.

docs.title: 1. Install the desktop app
docs.text:
• macOS

    brew install --cask openflocon/tap/flocon, or the DMG.

    Install on macOS

  • Linux

    .deb, .rpm (x64 and arm64), or Homebrew.

    Install on Linux

  • Windows

    The .msi installer.

    Install on Windows

docs.title: 2. Add the SDK to your app
docs.text:
• With your AI agent

    Install the Flocon plugin in Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, and let the agent set Flocon up in your project.

    Install with the Flocon plugin

  • Kotlin

    Android and Kotlin Multiplatform (Android, JVM, iOS, Wasm), one Gradle module per feature.

    Kotlin SDK

  • Swift

    iOS and macOS, with Swift Package Manager.

    Swift SDK

  • Flutter

    Android, iOS and macOS, one pub.dev package per feature.

    Flutter SDK

docs.title: 3. Connect
docs.text:
Start Flocon Desktop, then run your app.

  • Automatic

    Android emulator or USB device, iOS Simulator, macOS and JVM apps: nothing to do.

    Connect your app

  • Over Wi-Fi

    A physical device on the same network: give the SDK the address of your computer.

    Connect over Wi-Fi

  • With a QR code

    Scan the QR code shown by Flocon Desktop from your app.

    Connect with a QR code

Something not showing up? See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: 🗝️ Preferences & DataStore Editor
docs.text: Flocon shows the key-value storage of your app (SharedPreferences, Jetpack DataStore, UserDefaults, the Keychain, Flutter shared_preferences, or a store of your own) and lets you edit values live from the desktop. It saves you from re-installing the app or writing debug screens to put it in a given state.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter SharedPreferences (auto-discovery, editable) ✅ n/a n/a n/a Jetpack DataStore (editable) ✅ ✅ (iOS, JVM, no Wasm) n/a n/a UserDefaults (editable) n/a ✅ (iOS, standard suite) ✅ (standard, plus suites you register) n/a Keychain n/a ❌ (use a custom FloconPreference) ✅ (opt-in, read-only by default) n/a shared_preferences (editable) n/a n/a n/a ✅ Custom store (FloconPreference) ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌
  • On JVM and Wasm nothing is detected automatically: register a store of your own.
  • Values of type String, Boolean, number and a set / list of strings can be edited. An edit is only applied when its type matches the stored one.

docs.title: Setup
Usage
Standard SharedPreferences (Android)
docs.text:
All the SharedPreferences files of the app are automatically detected on Android. To register one with a custom display name:

val userPrefs = context.getSharedPreferences("user_pref", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
Flocon.preferencesPlugin.register(FloconSharedPreference(name = "User Settings", userPrefs))

docs.title: Jetpack DataStore
docs.text:
Register your DataStore instance (Android, JVM and iOS):

val Context.dataStore by preferencesDataStore(name = "settings")

Flocon.preferencesPlugin.register(FloconDatastorePreference(name = "App Settings", context.dataStore))

If the values are encrypted, pass a FloconDatastoreMapper to decode / encode them:

FloconDatastorePreference(name = "Secure Settings", context.secureDataStore, mapper = myCipherMapper)

docs.title: UserDefaults (iOS)
docs.text: The standard UserDefaults of the app are listed automatically on iOS and can be edited.

docs.title: Custom key-value storage
docs.text:
You can expose any proprietary storage system (such as EncryptedSharedPreferences or custom key-value stores, on every platform) by implementing FloconPreference:

class MyCustomPreference : FloconPreference {
    override val name: String = "Encrypted Vault"
    override val type: String = "EncryptedSharedPreferences"

    override suspend fun columns(): List<String> = listOf("token", "is_authenticated")

    override suspend fun get(columnName: String): FloconPreferenceValue? {
        return FloconPreferenceValue(stringValue = readSecureKey(columnName))
    }

    override suspend fun set(columnName: String, value: FloconPreferenceValue) {
        writeSecureKey(columnName, value.stringValue)
    }
}

Flocon.preferencesPlugin.register(MyCustomPreference())

docs.title: Preference type
docs.text:
Each preference tells the desktop app which storage it comes from. The type is displayed with its icon next to the name in the preference selector (known types have their own icon, the others a generic one), and returned by the MCP list_shared_preferences tool.

The built-in preferences set it for you. For your own FloconPreference, override type with one of the FloconPreferenceType constants or any free value (defaults to "Custom"):

Constant Value Platform FloconPreferenceType.SharedPreferences SharedPreferences Android FloconPreferenceType.DataStore DataStore Android, iOS, JVM FloconPreferenceType.UserDefaults UserDefaults iOS FloconPreferenceType.Keychain Keychain iOS FloconPreferenceType.JavaPreferences Java Preferences JVM FloconPreferenceType.LocalStorage LocalStorage Wasm FloconPreferenceType.Custom Custom default

docs.title: UserDefaults suites
docs.text:
UserDefaults.standard is listed automatically. Register the other suites of your app, such as the one shared with an App Group:

let suiteName = "group.com.example.app"

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.preferences) { options in
        if let shared = UserDefaults(suiteName: suiteName) {
            options.userDefaults(shared, suiteName: suiteName)
        }
    }
}
#endif

or later: Flocon.preferencesPlugin.registerUserDefaults(shared, suiteName: suiteName).

Only the values written by your app are shown, not the system defaults. String, Bool, numbers, Date and [String] can be edited, other values (Data, dictionaries, mixed arrays) are read-only.

docs.title: Keychain
docs.text:
The Keychain is opt-in: its values are sent unencrypted to the Mac running Flocon, so only enable it in debug builds.

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.preferences) { options in
        options.keychain(isEditable: false)
    }
}
#endif

Generic and internet passwords appear as two stores, with one key per item (service / account and server / account). Values are shown as text when they are UTF-8, and as their size otherwise. Items protected by Face ID, Touch ID or the passcode are shown as <protected>: Flocon never shows an authentication prompt.

With isEditable: true, values edited and items deleted in the desktop are applied to the Keychain. Only existing items with a readable text value can be edited, items are never added.

docs.title: Custom key-value storage
docs.text:
Implement FloconPreference to show another store (a remote config, Realm, an in-memory cache...), then install or register it:

final class FeatureFlagsPreference: FloconPreference {
    let name = "Feature flags"
    let type = "Remote config"

    func keys() -> [String] { FeatureFlags.all.map(\.key) }

    func value(forKey key: String) -> FloconPreferenceValue? {
        FloconPreferenceValue(booleanValue: FeatureFlags.isEnabled(key))
    }

    func setValue(_ value: FloconPreferenceValue, forKey key: String) {
        if let isEnabled = value.booleanValue { FeatureFlags.set(key, isEnabled) }
    }

    // optional: lets the desktop delete keys
    func removeValue(forKey key: String) {}
}

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.preferences) { $0.preference(FeatureFlagsPreference()) }
}
#endif

The methods are called from a background thread. type defaults to FloconPreferenceType.custom, the other values are .userDefaults and .keychain, and any string is accepted.

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
• Preference selector: pick a store, with its type icon (SharedPreferences, DataStore, UserDefaults, Keychain, custom).
  • Keys list: key, type and value. Filter by key, and refresh automatically with the auto-update delay.
  • Edit: edit a value in the side panel and save it (Send to app, ⌘↵). Booleans and numbers have dedicated controls (increment / decrement), and string values that contain JSON get a Formatted / Raw view with a validity check.
  • Delete: delete a key, after confirmation. The key is removed from the app and this cannot be undone. Values the desktop cannot edit are marked read only.
  • Copy a key or a value.

Warning

Editing a value changes your app's real data and can lose data. The app does not always observe the change (a cached SharedPreferences value, a UserDefaults value already read): restart the screen or the app to see its effect.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_shared_preferences: the stores of the app (SharedPreferences files, UserDefaults suites), with their id and type.
  • get_shared_preference_values: the keys and values of a store, with their type.
  • set_shared_preference_value: edit one existing key (keys cannot be created or removed). The previous value is returned so it can be restored, and agents should ask you to confirm first.

Example prompt: "Set onboarding_done to false in the app preferences, then tell me the previous value."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Kotlin: nothing is detected automatically on JVM and Wasm, and DataStore is not available on Wasm.
  • Swift: the Keychain is opt-in and read-only unless isEditable: true; Data and dictionary values of UserDefaults are read-only.
  • Flutter: only shared_preferences is supported for now.

docs.title: 📋 Structured Data Tables
docs.text:
Tables let your app stream rows of multi-column data to Flocon Desktop. You name a table, log rows with the columns you want, and the desktop builds the table for you: no model to declare, columns are created from the names you use.

Common use cases:

  • Inspect active in-memory user sessions or authentication states.
  • Stream custom business domain telemetry.
  • Monitor cache keys and eviction events.
  • Track queued background jobs or workers.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Log table rows ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

Values are always strings: format numbers and dates yourself before logging them.

docs.title: Setup
Usage
docs.text:
Each call logs one row in the named table. Rows are appended in real time, with the time they were logged.

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.Flocon
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.tables.dsl.table
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.tables.tablePlugin

Flocon.tablePlugin.table("active_sessions") {
    column("user_id", "1024")
    column("name", "Raphael")
    column("status", "Active")
    column("last_seen", "2026-08-14 17:30")
}

Flocon.tablePlugin.table("active_sessions").log(
    TableColumnConfig("user_id", "1024"),
    TableColumnConfig("name", "Raphael"),
    TableColumnConfig("status", "Active"),
    TableColumnConfig("last_seen", "2026-08-14 17:30")
)

log also takes an array: log([TableColumnConfig]).

Flocon.table.table('active_sessions').log([
  TableColumnConfig('user_id', '1024'),
  TableColumnConfig('name', 'Raphael'),
  TableColumnConfig('status', 'Active'),
  TableColumnConfig('last_seen', '2026-08-14 17:30'),
]);

docs.title: Real-time event tracking
docs.text:
Log a row each time something happens to follow it live:

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
fun onUserAction(user: User, action: String) {
    Flocon.tablePlugin.table("user_actions") {
        column("timestamp", System.currentTimeMillis().toString())
        column("user", user.name)
        column("action", action)
    }
}

func onUserAction(user: User, action: String) {
    Flocon.tablePlugin.table("user_actions").log(
        TableColumnConfig("timestamp", String(Date().timeIntervalSince1970)),
        TableColumnConfig("user", user.name),
        TableColumnConfig("action", action)
    )
}

void onUserAction(User user, String action) {
  Flocon.table.table('user_actions').log([
    TableColumnConfig('timestamp', DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch.toString()),
    TableColumnConfig('user', user.name),
    TableColumnConfig('action', action),
  ]);
}

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

Each row also shows up in the Timeline.

Open Tables in the sidebar.

  • The Table selector at the top switches between the tables your app logged.
  • The filter field keeps the rows where a value contains the text.
  • The columns are the names used in the logged rows. Click a row to read all its columns in the detail panel, where they can be copied.
  • Right-click a row to Remove it or Remove lines above.
  • The trash icon clears the rows of the table, and the overflow menu has Export CSV.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_tables: the tables sent by the app, with their tableId.
  • list_table_items: the rows of a table (newest first), as column name to value maps, with optional text filter, order and limit.

"Look at the active_sessions table and tell me which users have not been seen for more than an hour."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Telemetry & Privacy
docs.text:
Flocon Desktop can send a small amount of usage statistics, only if you opt in, so maintainers know which features are actually used and on which platforms. This page lists exactly what is collected.

Nothing from your apps is ever sent

Flocon is a debugging tool: it sees network calls, databases, preferences and files of the apps you inspect. None of it leaves your computer. No URLs, payloads, headers, package names, device names or database content are ever part of an event.

The SDKs in your app (Kotlin, Swift, Flutter) collect and send nothing: telemetry is a Flocon Desktop setting only. The only SDK information that is reported is its kind and version, when an app connects (device_connected).

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
On first launch, a card asks you to pick a level. Nothing is sent until you answer: as long as you haven't chosen, telemetry stays disabled. You can change your choice at any time in Settings → Privacy.

Level What it means Anonymous (opt-in) A random identifier is generated in memory at each launch and never written to disk. Flocon can count sessions and feature usage, but cannot recognise you across launches. Full (opt-in) A random identifier is stored on your computer so returning users can be counted. Switching back to Anonymous or Disabled deletes it. Disabled Nothing is sent. This is also the behaviour until you answer the consent card.

Telemetry is also fully disabled when:

  • the DO_NOT_TRACK environment variable is set (any value other than empty, 0 or false), following consoledonottrack.com;
  • you build Flocon yourself or use a fork: only official releases contain the analytics key;
  • Flocon runs in mock mode (--mock=<scenario>).

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Event When Extra properties app_started Once per launch, if you opted in before A snapshot of a few settings, see below screen_viewed A menu entry or a sub-screen is opened, at most once per screen per launch screen: a menu entry (e.g. Network, Database) or NetworkMocks, NetworkBadQuality, NetworkDetail screen_empty_shown The empty state of a page is displayed (nothing to show yet), at most once per page per launch screen: the documentation page (Network, Database, Timeline...) mcp_used An MCP tool is called, at most once per tool per launch (list_devices is not tracked: it is called every time) tool: the fixed tool name (e.g. list_network_calls), client: claude, cursor, codex, windsurf, vscode, zed, other or unknown. Never the arguments or the results of the call feature_used A bounded list of actions is used (see below). The core action of each screen is sent at most once per launch feature, screen, and when relevant value (true/false), source, enabled_mocks_count setting_changed One of a few settings is changed setting, value (true/false, or graph/list), screen device_connected An app with the Flocon SDK connects, at most once per device and app per launch (the app relaunches on every build) platform (android, ios, desktop, other), sdk (kotlin, swift, flutter, other, unknown), sdk_version (unknown when it is not a version), connection_type (default, wifi, unknown). Only known values are sent. Never the device name, the app name or its package

docs.title: app_started properties
docs.text:
Only booleans, counts and fixed values, never a name or a configuration value. A value that can't be read quickly is left out.

Property Values timeline_view graph, list timeline_auto_scroll, timeline_screenshots, timeline_merge_plugins true, false mascot_enabled true, false enabled_mocks_count number of enabled network mocks of the selected app (left out when no app is selected yet) bad_network_enabled true if a bad network configuration is enabled for the selected app (left out when no app is selected yet)

docs.title: feature_used and setting_changed
docs.text:
screen takes the same values as screen_viewed: NetworkMocks, NetworkBadQuality, NetworkDetail, Timeline, Settings, Database, Deeplinks, SharedPreferences, FeatureFlags, Files, AdbCommander, TopBar.

feature Screen Notes mock_create_clicked, mock_imported, mock_exported NetworkMocks mock_toggled NetworkMocks value = enabled, enabled_mocks_count after the change bad_network_create_clicked NetworkBadQuality bad_network_toggled NetworkBadQuality value = a configuration is now enabled detail_open_externally_request, detail_open_externally_response, detail_share_markdown, detail_save_html, detail_copy_curl, detail_copy_text, detail_copy_image, detail_save_image, detail_diff_with_clipboard, detail_json_detail, detail_bearer_jwt NetworkDetail Only which action, never the content database_query_executed Database Once per launch. Never the query deeplink_launched Deeplinks Once per launch. Never the deeplink shared_preference_edited SharedPreferences Once per launch. Never the key or the value file_opened Files Once per launch. Never the path adb_command_sent AdbCommander Once per launch. Never the command screenshot_taken, video_recorded TopBar Once per launch help_opened the documentation page (Network, Database, Timeline... or Setup) source: top_bar, empty_state, empty_state_no_device setting Screen value timeline_view Timeline graph, list timeline_auto_scroll, timeline_screenshots, timeline_merge_plugins Timeline true, false mascot_enabled Settings true, false

Every event also carries: Flocon version, OS name and architecture, the telemetry level, and the per-launch session id.

docs.title: Where the data goes
docs.text:
Events are sent to PostHog Cloud in the EU region. No person profiles are created, IP geolocation is disabled, and the PostHog project is configured to discard client IP addresses.

The full implementation lives in FloconDesktop/composeApp/.../telemetry.

docs.title: For contributors
docs.text:
• Add events only through TelemetryManager.track(...) and list them in TelemetryEvents and on this page.
  • Never pass data coming from the inspected apps.
  • The key is injected at build time from the POSTHOG_API_KEY environment variable (a GitHub secret on the release workflow). Without it, the app compiles and telemetry is a no-op. To test locally against your own PostHog project: POSTHOG_API_KEY=phc_xxx ./gradlew run.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: title: Timeline description: Follow everything your app did, in order, on a single screen: network calls, analytics, database queries, crashes...

docs.title: 🕒 Timeline
docs.text: The timeline merges the events received by Flocon Desktop into one chronological list, grouped by day and by app session, so you can see what happened right before a crash or an HTTP error. Your app can also push its own events into it (screens, user actions, lifecycle, milestones).

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Merged view of the other plugins (desktop only, nothing to install) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Logs from your app (navigation, userAction, lifecycle, custom) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Automatic navigation / lifecycle logging ❌ ❌ ❌ ✅ (FloconNavigatorObserver, FloconLifecycleObserver)

Each source of the timeline only shows up once its plugin is installed in your app. On Kotlin, Swift and Flutter the logs are sent by your own calls: Flocon does not detect screens or taps by itself, except with the two Flutter observers below.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The timeline itself needs nothing: it is built on the desktop from the events of the other plugins. Each source appears once its plugin is installed, see:

  • Network
  • Analytics
  • Databases
  • Data Tables
  • Crash Reporter
  • Deeplinks
  • WebViews
  • Logs from your app

To send your own logs, install the timeline plugin:

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
dependencies {
    debugImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-timeline:LAST_VERSION")
    releaseImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-timeline-no-op:LAST_VERSION")
}

startFlocon(FloconContext(applicationContext)) {
    install(FloconTimeline)
}

A plugin that is not installed does nothing instead of crashing.

import Flocon

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { flocon in
    flocon.install(.timeline)
}
#endif

Flocon.initialize() installs every plugin, the timeline included. Until Flocon is started, or if .timeline is not installed, the calls do nothing.

flutter pub add flocon

The timeline is part of the flocon package and is registered by startFlocon: there is nothing to install.

import 'package:flocon/flocon.dart';

await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon..connect(host: 'localhost')); // 10.0.2.2 from the Android emulator

Tip

Start with Getting Started to connect your app to Flocon Desktop.

docs.title: Logs from your app
docs.text:
Besides the events of the other plugins, your app can push its own events into the timeline, to read what happened around a bug: which screen was open, what the user did, what the app lifecycle was, and any milestone of your own.

There are two kinds of calls, never mixed:

  • Typed, without level: log with a type, and the shortcuts logNavigation, logUserAction and logLifecycle.
  • Tagged, with a level: the tag is the type of the event, and the level is Debug, Info, Warning or Error.

value is the main text of the row (a screen name for example), params is a string-to-string map shown in the detail panel (text only, optional).

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.Flocon
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.timeline.*
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.timeline.model.*

Flocon.timelinePlugin.logNavigation("CheckoutScreen", params = mapOf("from" to "CartScreen"))
Flocon.timelinePlugin.logUserAction("Tap on Pay")
Flocon.timelinePlugin.logLifecycle("App moved to background")

// a custom tag, with a level
Flocon.timelinePlugin.log("payment", "Card declined", mapOf("code" to "402"), FloconTimelineLevel.Warning)

Navigation listener (Compose)

import androidx.compose.runtime.Composable
import androidx.compose.runtime.DisposableEffect
import androidx.navigation.NavController
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.Flocon
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.timeline.*

@Composable
fun NavigationLogger(navController: NavController) {
    DisposableEffect(navController) {
        val listener = NavController.OnDestinationChangedListener { _, destination, arguments ->
            Flocon.timelinePlugin.logNavigation(
                value = destination.route ?: "unknown",
                // string arguments only
                params = arguments?.let { b -> b.keySet().associateWith { b.getString(it).orEmpty() } }.orEmpty(),
            )
        }
        navController.addOnDestinationChangedListener(listener)
        onDispose { navController.removeOnDestinationChangedListener(listener) }
    }
}

Define your own type. Declare it once and reuse it, optionally with an extension:

import io.github.openflocon.flocon.Flocon
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.timeline.*
import io.github.openflocon.flocon.timeline.model.*

val Billing = FloconTimelineType("billing")

fun FloconTimelinePlugin.logBilling(value: String, params: Map<String, String> = emptyMap()) =
    log(Billing, value, params)

Flocon.timelinePlugin.logBilling("Subscription started", mapOf("sku" to "premium_yearly"))

import Flocon

// typed events, without a level
Flocon.timelinePlugin.logNavigation("CheckoutScreen", params: ["from": "CartScreen"])
Flocon.timelinePlugin.logUserAction("tap_buy", params: ["sku": "premium_yearly"])
Flocon.timelinePlugin.logLifecycle("didBecomeActive")

// tagged event, with a level: .debug, .info (default), .warning or .error
Flocon.timelinePlugin.log(tag: "billing", value: "Purchase failed", params: ["sku": "premium_yearly"], level: .error)

Define your own type. Declare it once and reuse it:

extension TimelineType {
    static let billing = TimelineType("billing")
}

Flocon.timelinePlugin.log(type: .billing, value: "Purchase started")

See also the FloconSwift README.

import 'package:flocon/flocon.dart';

// typed events, without a level
Flocon.timeline.logNavigation('CheckoutScreen', params: {'from': 'CartScreen'});
Flocon.timeline.logUserAction('tap_buy');
Flocon.timeline.logLifecycle('App moved to background');

// tagged event, with a level: TimelineLevel.debug, info (default), warning or error
Flocon.timeline.logTagged('payment', 'Card declined', params: {'code': '402'}, level: TimelineLevel.warning);

// a custom type, without a level
Flocon.timeline.log(const TimelineType('billing'), 'Subscription started');

Automatic navigation and lifecycle logs. Add the observer to your navigator (MaterialApp, GoRouter...) and start the lifecycle observer:

MaterialApp(
  navigatorObservers: [FloconNavigatorObserver()],
  // ...
);

FloconLifecycleObserver.start(); // logs each AppLifecycleState (resumed, paused...)

FloconNavigatorObserver logs push, pop and replace, with from and action in the params.

Note

The reserved types are navigation, userAction and lifecycle (matched without case sensitivity). A tag equal to one of them is shown as that type.

Note

Typed logs (navigation, user action, lifecycle and your own types) have no level on the wire: the desktop stores them as Info (a custom type shows as an Info diamond) and hides the level in their detail. The Level filter only applies to tagged logs: unticking Info does not hide navigation, user action or lifecycle logs.

A new type shows up by itself as a value of the Type filter: the desktop does not need an update. The wire format is described in the protocol.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
From the desktop UI, you can:

  • Follow the events in order: network calls (a request line with a → arrow, then a response line with a ← arrow when it arrives; selecting or hovering one highlights both, and hovering shows a bar linking them), analytics events, WebView events (console messages, page loads and errors, bridge calls), database queries, table rows, logs sent by your app, crashes, deeplinks, ADB commands and app starts.
  • Switch between the list and the graph (the List and Graph chips next to the filter bar, the choice is remembered), see Graph.
  • Read the counters: number of events, sessions, HTTP errors and crashes of what is displayed.
  • Options (⋮ menu): auto scroll to the newest event, invert the direction of the list, pin the detail panel (it then stays next to the list instead of covering it).
  • Filter: toggle the sources (the selection is remembered) and search a text (Ctrl+K / Cmd+K focuses the search field).
  • Open an event: click a row to open its detail in a side panel (network call, analytics event, log, database query, table row, crash, deeplink, ADB command). App starts and WebView events have nothing to open: the WebViews screen shows them.

docs.title: Graph
docs.text:
The Graph view shows one session at a time on a time axis, with the app start at 0. The filters and the selected event are shared with the list.

  • One lane per type: App, Analytics, Network, Logs, Database (a lane without event is hidden). The other sources only appear in the list.
  • One graph instead of lanes: the switch left of List / Graph in the top bar (the choice is remembered) puts every type in the same rows, one under the other, packed as tightly as possible. The graph is much shorter, and what happened around a moment is read in one vertical slice. A type is told by its color, the column on the left becomes the legend.
  • A network call is one bar, from its request to its response. The method and an image icon are shown when the bar is wide enough, and a failed call (HTTP 4xx or 5xx) is red, like a log with the Error level. A call still waiting for its response (or a stream that never ends) is not drawn.
  • Database queries, analytics events and logs are diamonds: they have no duration.
  • Events that do not overlap share the same row, to keep the graph short.
Action Result Click a bar or a diamond Opens the event in the detail panel and selects it in the list too Mouse wheel Scrolls the lanes Ctrl / Cmd + wheel, + / - buttons Zooms around the pointer Shift + wheel, drag Moves along the time axis Fit Shows the whole session again and follows the new events ‹ / › Previous / next session

docs.title: Grouped events
docs.text:
Events closer than about 14 px on the graph are merged into one rounded marker, so a burst of 100 events takes one slot of a row instead of 100 rows.

  • The marker is cut in one segment per type (in the order of the lanes), each as wide as its share of the events (never under 8 %), with the same colors as the lanes. The total number of events is written on top. A marker with failed events has a small red badge on its top right corner with their number, and the failed events are tinted red in the popover.
  • Click a marker to open a popover: the number of events and the time the group spans, then one chip per type with its count (click a chip to hide or show that type), and the list of every event of the group in start order, filtered by the chips. Each row gives the time since the start of the group, the type, the duration, the name and the status code of a network call; click a row to open the event in the detail panel. Zoom on the group zooms on it, Show every event opens the group into rows, like without grouping: it is the way to see events at the very same instant, which no zoom can separate. Turning the option off and on again groups them back.
  • Zooming in splits the markers, until each event is back to its own bar or diamond. Events are grouped by their start, whatever their duration.
  • Turn it off with Cluster close events in the overflow menu of the timeline (on by default, remembered).

docs.title: Logs sent by your app
docs.text:
• Logs are a Log source, in the list and in the graph (one marker per log, in its own lane).
  • Filter them in the Logs card of the filter panel, see Logs filters.
  • The same shape and color are used in the list, the graph, the detail and the filters (shapes and lightness differ, so they do not rely on color alone):
Log Shape Color navigation right arrow green userAction mouse pointer cyan lifecycle heart red-pink Tagged or custom type, Debug diamond dark blue Tagged or custom type, Info diamond pale violet Tagged or custom type, Warning diamond orange Tagged or custom type, Error diamond red
  • Click a row to open its detail: value, type, level, params and time.
  • The desktop keeps at most 20 000 logs per device and app, the oldest ones are dropped first.

docs.title: Logs filters
docs.text:
The Logs card of the filter panel (shown while the Log source is selected) has three filters:

  • Types: one menu to show or hide Navigation, User action, Lifecycle and Tagged logs (every log whose type is not one of the three, your custom types included), each with its count. When some are hidden, the menu shows the types still shown as chips (the x hides one).
  • Tag: type a word and press Enter (or +) to keep the tagged logs whose tag contains it, or − to hide them. The match is a case-insensitive "contains". The known tags are suggested while you type, each with + and −. The rules are listed under Includes and Excludes, with a checkbox to switch one off without deleting it.
  • Level: Debug, Info, Warning and Error, with their counts.

The Tag and Level filters only apply to tagged logs: navigation, user action and lifecycle logs are never hidden by them. Unticking Tagged logs hides every tagged log and locks (dims) the Tag and Level filters.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• get_timeline: reads a window of the timeline (the latest crash, the last minutes, a session, around a time or an event id), with a text search over the events.
  • show_in_timeline: moves the desktop window to the timeline (graph view) and centers it on an event, a time, or the latest crash.

"Show me what happened in the minute before the last crash, and tell me which network call failed."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No custom icon or color per tag: custom tags use a default style.
  • params are text only, not nested.
  • No clear button for the logs: they are removed with the device or app data.
  • It is not a replacement for analytics events, which keep their own plugin.

docs.title: 🚨 Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with the basics, they explain most cases:

  • Flocon Desktop is running before the app starts (the SDK retries every 3 seconds, so starting it later also works).
  • The SDK is started (startFlocon was called) and the feature you look for is installed.
  • The SDK and the desktop are on the same major version (the connection is encrypted with wss:// / https://, an old SDK cannot reach a new desktop).
  • Turn on the SDK logs to see the connection attempts: FloconLogger.enabled = true (Kotlin), Flocon.isLoggingEnabled = true (Swift, Flutter), set before starting.

docs.title: Android emulator or USB device
docs.text:
The SDK connects to localhost and the desktop runs adb reverse so that the ports reach your computer. No cleartext or networkSecurityConfig entry is needed.

adb devices
  • The device must be listed as device. If it says unauthorized, accept the USB debugging prompt on the phone.
  • adb must be in your PATH (see the macOS, Linux or Windows guide).
  • Several devices or restarted emulator: unplug, run adb kill-server, then adb devices again.
  • Flutter on an Android emulator: use the host 10.0.2.2 in connect(host: ...), see Connect your app.

docs.title: iOS: the local network permission
docs.text:
On a physical device, iOS asks the user to allow the app to find devices on the local network, and needs NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription in Info.plist (Swift and Flutter apps, and Kotlin Multiplatform iOS apps).

  • No prompt and no connection: the key is missing. Add it and reinstall the app.
  • You tapped "Don't Allow": enable it again in Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network (or in the settings of your app).
  • The iOS Simulator and macOS apps connect to localhost and need nothing special. The macOS Flutter app also needs the com.apple.security.network.client entitlement, and Android Flutter apps the INTERNET permission.

docs.title: Physical device over Wi-Fi
docs.text:
There is no adb reverse for Wi-Fi: the app must be given the IP address of your computer, and both must be on the same network.

  • Give the address with connect { address = "..." } / Flocon.connect(...), or scan the QR code of the desktop Connect dialog. See Connect over Wi-Fi and Connect with a QR code.
  • Guest or corporate Wi-Fi often isolates devices from each other ("client isolation"): use a personal hotspot or USB for Android.
  • A VPN or a firewall on your computer can block the ports 9023 and 9024.
  • The address has no scheme and no path: 192.168.1.20 or 192.168.1.20:9023:9024.

docs.title: Connection fails after changing ports
docs.text:
If you changed the ports in Settings > Server ports, or launched the desktop with --websocket-port / --http-port, the SDK must use the same ones, except on an Android emulator or USB device where adb reverse maps the default 9023 / 9024 to the desktop ports. Everywhere else (device over Wi-Fi, iOS, JVM, Wasm, Flutter) set the ports in the SDK, otherwise the app silently never connects. See Ports.

Desktop ports must be in 1024-65535, different from each other, and not 9042.

docs.title: The MCP port is taken
docs.text: The MCP server of the desktop always listens on port 9042 and this cannot be changed. If another program uses it, Flocon Desktop logs Cannot start MCP server on port 9042 and retries every 10 seconds: close the other program (find it with lsof -i :9042 on macOS and Linux). Your SDK connection is not affected. See MCP.

docs.title: The "SDK update" banner
docs.text: A badge SDK x -> y in the top bar of Flocon Desktop means the connected app runs an older SDK than the latest release. Click it to see the versions and the release notes. Update the SDK in your app (and keep the desktop up to date too): an SDK older than the desktop may miss features or fail to connect. You can ignore the notice from the same popup.

docs.title: Web (Kotlin/Wasm)
docs.text: The browser rejects the self-signed certificate of the desktop: open https://localhost:9023 once (use your websocket port) in the browser and accept the certificate.

docs.title: Something is connected but a screen is empty
docs.text:
• The feature is not installed in the SDK (install(...)), or the Kotlin module is a -no-op in the build you run. The desktop only shows the menu entries of the installed plugins.
  • The feature is not supported on your platform: check the table of the home page and the support table of the feature page.
  • Wrong build variant: in Kotlin, the real modules are debugImplementation; a release build runs the no-ops.

docs.title: 💬 WebSockets
docs.text:
Flocon shows the WebSocket traffic of your app next to its HTTP calls: when a connection opens, every message sent and received, errors and closings. It helps with live feeds, chats and multiplayer events, where the bug is often in a frame you cannot see.

For every connection, Flocon records:

  • Lifecycle: the URL, open, closing, closed and error events.
  • Messages: the text of each message sent and received, with its size.
  • Order and time: events in the order they happened, with their timestamp.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Automatic capture ✅ OkHttp listener ✅ OkHttp listener (JVM only), otherwise manual ❌ manual ❌ manual Manual logging ✅ ✅ ✅ logWebSocketEvent ✅ Flocon.network.logWebSocketEvent Inject a message (mock) ✅ ✅ JVM (OkHttp) ❌ ❌
  • On Android with OkHttp, wrap your listener to log the incoming frames, and send with a Flocon helper to log the outgoing ones. Other WebSocket clients (Ktor, URLSessionWebSocketTask, web_socket_channel) are not intercepted: log their events yourself.
  • Binary messages are logged as text (ByteString.toString() on OkHttp).
  • Only the OkHttp listener (listenWithFlocon) can receive messages injected from the desktop side. The MCP tools describe it as Android only for now.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
WebSocket events go through the network plugin: follow the network setup first.

KotlinSwiftFlutter 
startFlocon(FloconContext(context)) {
    install(FloconNetwork)
}

The OkHttp helpers are in the flocon-okhttp-interceptor module (Android and JVM):

dependencies {
    debugImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core:LAST_VERSION")
    releaseImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-network-core-no-op:LAST_VERSION")
    debugImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-okhttp-interceptor:LAST_VERSION")
    releaseImplementation("io.github.openflocon:flocon-okhttp-interceptor-no-op:LAST_VERSION")
}

#if DEBUG
startFlocon { $0.install(.network) }
#endif

await startFlocon((flocon) => flocon..install(FloconNetwork()));

docs.title: Usage
Inject a message (Android)
docs.text:
On Android and JVM (OkHttp), a connection created with listenWithFlocon(id = ...) registers itself with the desktop. You can then inject a text message into it, as if the server had sent it, to see how your app reacts to a payload you choose. The message goes through your own listener (onMessage).

This is done from an AI agent with the MCP tools below (their description says Android, the JVM works the same way). The Swift and Flutter SDKs do not support it.

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

WebSocket events also show up in the Timeline, next to the other network calls.

WebSocket events appear in the Network list, with the other calls:

  • the type column shows a WebSocket tag, with an up arrow for a message sent and a down arrow for a message received;
  • open, closing, closed and error events have their own line;
  • click an event to see its message and size in the detail panel, with the JSON viewer for JSON payloads.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_network_calls: includes the WebSocket events, with their messages in the detail.
  • list_websocket_clients: lists the ids of the connections that accept injected messages.
  • send_websocket_message: injects a text message into one of them.

"Send {\"type\":\"price\",\"value\":0} to the prices socket and tell me what the app shows."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Only OkHttp WebSockets on Android are captured without code on your side; every other case is logged by hand.
  • Mocking WebSocket messages is Android only, with listenWithFlocon.
  • Binary frames are logged as text.

docs.title: 🌐 WebView Viewer
docs.text: Flocon displays what happens inside the WebViews of your application: the JS console, the page loads and errors, and the calls from the page to your native code. No more chrome://inspect and USB debugging to read a console.error.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
The WebView plugin is available in the Kotlin / KMP SDK only. The Swift and Flutter SDKs do not have it yet.

Android KMP (iOS / JVM / Wasm) Swift (iOS / macOS) Flutter Automatic capture (attach) ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ Manual API (logConsole, logPageEvent, logBridgeCall) ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌

On iOS, JVM and Wasm (Kotlin) there is no attach yet: use the manual API. The requests made by the page (fetch, XMLHttpRequest) are not captured yet.

docs.title: Setup
Usage
docs.text:
KotlinSwiftFlutter

Attach a WebView (Android). Attach each WebView once, after you set your own WebViewClient / WebChromeClient:

webView.settings.javaScriptEnabled = true
webView.webViewClient = MyWebViewClient()
webView.webChromeClient = MyWebChromeClient()

Flocon.webViewPlugin.attach(webView, webViewId = "checkout")

attach wraps your clients: every callback is still forwarded to them, so the behavior of your WebView does not change. The wrappers are read back from the WebView on Android 8.0 (API 26) and above. Below, wrap your clients yourself:

webView.webViewClient = FloconWebViewClient(Flocon.webViewPlugin, "checkout", delegate = MyWebViewClient())
webView.webChromeClient = FloconWebChromeClient(Flocon.webViewPlugin, "checkout", webView, delegate = MyWebChromeClient())

Bridge calls. Flocon cannot see the calls made to an object you expose with addJavascriptInterface: log them from the method itself.

class AppBridge {
    @JavascriptInterface
    fun share(text: String): String {
        val result = shareUseCase(text)
        Flocon.webViewPlugin.logBridgeCall(
            webViewId = "checkout",
            interfaceName = "Android",
            method = "share",
            arguments = text,
            result = result,
        )
        return result
    }
}

Manual API. The same functions are available on every Kotlin platform, for a WebView Flocon does not attach to:

Flocon.webViewPlugin.logConsole(webViewId = "checkout", level = WebViewConsoleLevel.Warn, message = "slow render")
Flocon.webViewPlugin.logPageEvent(webViewId = "checkout", type = WebViewPageEventType.PageFinished, url = "https://example.com")

Not available in the Swift SDK yet

Not available in the Flutter SDK yet

docs.title: In Flocon Desktop
docs.text:
In the Timeline

Console messages, page loads and bridge calls also show up in the Timeline.

The WebViews screen lists three kinds of events, newest first:

  • Console: console.log, info, warn and error of the page, with the source file and line when the browser gives them
  • Pages: page started / finished, navigation, and the errors (network error, HTTP error, SSL error)
  • Bridge: the calls from the page to a native object exposed with addJavascriptInterface, with their arguments and result

Filter by kind with the chips at the top (All, Console, Pages, Bridge), or search in the level, message, url and WebView id. Each WebView is identified by the id you give it, so several WebViews of the same app can be told apart. The events also show up in the timeline as a WebView source.

docs.title: With AI agents (MCP)
docs.text:
• list_webview_events: the console, page and bridge events of the WebViews, newest first.

"Is there a JS error in the checkout WebView? Read the console events."

See the MCP cookbook for full workflows.

docs.title: 🪟 Install on Windows
docs.text:
Download the .msi installer (Flocon-<version>.msi, x64) from the releases page and run it. Flocon then starts from the Start menu.

Download Flocon Desktop

A portable jar is also attached (Flocon-windows-x64.jar); it needs a JDK 21 to run.

docs.title: adb
docs.text:
To reach Android emulators and USB devices, Flocon Desktop needs adb in your PATH. It comes with the Android SDK platform-tools (installed with Android Studio, in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk\platform-tools): add that folder to your PATH, then check:

adb devices
